This gives p prime equal to approximately 0.17.
So in one generation, the allele frequency increases from 0.10 to about 0.17.
The key idea is that selection acts on genotypes, but allele frequencies change because genotypes differ in reproductive success.

title: Introduction to Population Genetics
text:
Forms of Selection


Natural selection

Directional selection

Allele frequency moves toward fixation or loss

Positive selection: favors beneficial alleles

Purifying selection: removes deleterious alleles


Balancing selection

Maintains multiple alleles in the population

Example: heterozygote advantage

Produces stable equilibrium allele frequencies


Artificial selection
Selection imposed by humans.

Individuals with desired traits are chosen

Those individuals contribute more offspring

Favored alleles increase in frequency

Examples:

Dog breeds

Dairy cattle

Crop varieties

Artificial selection = natural selection
directed by humans.


Natural selection can operate in several different ways.
Directional selection changes allele frequencies in a consistent direction.
Positive selection increases the frequency of beneficial alleles, sometimes leading to fixation.
Purifying selection, also called negative selection, removes deleterious alleles from the population.
Both of these are forms of directional selection.
Balancing selection operates differently.
Instead of eliminating one allele, it maintains multiple alleles within the population.
A classic example is heterozygote advantage, where heterozygotes have higher fitness than either homozygote.
In this case, selection maintains a stable equilibrium of allele frequencies.
Selection can also be imposed by humans.
In artificial selection, individuals with desirable traits are chosen to reproduce.
Over generations, alleles associated with those traits increase in frequency.
Dogs, dairy cattle, and many crop varieties are products of artificial selection.
The genetic mechanism is the same as natural selection. The difference is that humans decide which traits are favored.

title: Introduction to Population Genetics
text:
Selective Sweep and Genetic Variation




Figure 18-22
Haplotypes before and after
a beneficial allele (red)
sweeps to fixation.

After selection:

Reduced genetic diversity

Increased linkage disequilibrium

One dominant haplotype



This figure illustrates a selective sweep.
Before selection, many different haplotypes exist in the population, and genetic diversity is high in the region.
A new beneficial mutation appears, shown in red.
Because the mutation increases fitness, natural selection drives it rapidly toward fixation.
The mutation originates on a single chromosome, so nearby alleles on that chromosome are carried along with it.
This process is called genetic hitchhiking.
As the beneficial allele spreads, the surrounding chromosomal segment also becomes common in the population.
As a result, genetic diversity near the selected site decreases, and one dominant haplotype becomes common.
At the same time, linkage disequilibrium increases, because nearby alleles are strongly associated.
Farther from the selected site, recombination breaks these associations, and genetic diversity gradually returns.
The key idea is that positive selection can reduce genetic variation locally, creating a characteristic genomic signature of low diversity and high linkage disequilibrium.

title: Introduction to Population Genetics
text:
Selective Sweep and Genetic Variation




Figure 18-23. Gene diversity near the SLC24A5 locus on chromosome 15.

Gene diversity is strongly reduced in Europeans
around the SLC24A5 locus.
This pattern is consistent with
a recent selective sweep.


This figure shows a real genomic example of a selective sweep.
The horizontal axis shows genomic position along a region of chromosome 15.
The vertical axis shows gene diversity, which measures the probability that two randomly chosen alleles differ.
The gene SLC24A5 is located near the center of this region. This gene is involved in skin pigmentation.
In European populations, gene diversity drops sharply around this locus.
In contrast, African, East Asian, and Native American populations show much higher diversity in the same region.
This pattern is consistent with a recent selective sweep in European populations.
A beneficial mutation increased rapidly in frequency, and nearby alleles were carried along with it. This process is called genetic hitchhiking.
Because the sweep occurred relatively recently, recombination has not yet restored genetic variation around the selected site.
The key idea is that strong positive selection can produce a localized reduction in genetic diversity.

title: Introduction to Population Genetics
section: Examples of Natural Selection in Humans
text:
Examples of Natural Selection in Humans








Gene
Trait / Function
Population(s)




G6PD
Malaria resistance
African populations


HBB (β-globin)
Malaria resistance (sickle-cell trait)
African, Mediterranean, South Asian populations


CCR5
Reduced susceptibility to HIV
European populations


LCT
Lactase persistence (milk digestion)
European and some African populations


SLC24A5
Skin pigmentation
European populations


MHC
Infectious disease resistance
Multiple populations




These genes show evidence of recent natural selection.

This table shows several well-known examples of natural selection in human populations.
Many involve resistance to infectious diseases.
For example, variants in the G6PD gene and in the HBB gene, which includes the sickle-cell allele, provide protection against malaria.
In the case of sickle-cell, heterozygotes gain protection against malaria, while homozygotes can develop severe disease. This is a classic example of balancing selection.
Other examples involve adaptation to diet.
The LCT gene allows adults to digest lactose. In populations with a long history of dairy farming, alleles for adult milk digestion increased in frequency.
This illustrates gene–culture coevolution.
SLC24A5 provides an example related to skin pigmentation. Allele frequencies vary geographically, consistent with adaptation to different levels of ultraviolet radiation.
Finally, the MHC region shows very high genetic diversity across human populations, reflecting balancing selection driven by infectious disease.
The key message is that natural selection has shaped human genetic variation in the recent past, and evolutionary processes continue to operate today.

title: Introduction to Population Genetics
text:
Balancing Selection Maintains Genetic Diversity




Figure 18-24
Number of SNPs along chromosome 6.

The MHC region shows a pronounced spike
of unusually high genetic diversity.

Key idea:
Balancing selection can maintain multiple alleles at a locus.


Directional selection often reduces genetic diversity.
When a beneficial allele sweeps to fixation, nearby genetic variation is lost.
Balancing selection has the opposite effect.
Instead of eliminating variation, it maintains multiple alleles in the population.
This figure shows the number of SNPs along a region of chromosome 6.
Most regions of the genome show moderate levels of diversity.
However, the MHC region shows a striking spike of unusually high genetic diversity.
The MHC, or Major Histocompatibility Complex, contains genes involved in immune recognition.
One explanation for this elevated diversity is heterozygote advantage.
Individuals carrying two different MHC alleles may recognize a wider range of pathogens.
As a result, selection favors maintaining multiple alleles rather than fixing a single variant.
The key idea is that balancing selection maintains genetic diversity at the selected locus.
This pattern is the opposite of a selective sweep.

title: Introduction to Population Genetics
text:
Mutation Maintains Genetic Variation


Neutral Variation: Mutation vs Drift

Mutation creates new alleles

Genetic drift removes variation

In small populations:

Drift is strong

Diversity is low

In large populations:

Drift is weak

Diversity is higher


Key idea:
Genetic diversity reflects a balance between mutation and drift.

Deleterious Alleles: Mutation vs Selection

Mutation continuously creates harmful alleles

Natural selection removes them


Even harmful alleles persist at low frequency
because mutation never stops.

Stronger selection → lower frequency
Higher mutation rate → higher frequency

Key idea:
Mutation prevents genetic variation from disappearing completely.


Mutation is the ultimate source of new genetic variation.
But why does variation not disappear, and why does it not increase indefinitely?
First, consider neutral variation.
Mutation introduces new alleles, while genetic drift removes variation through random sampling.
In small populations, drift is strong, so genetic diversity tends to be low.
In large populations, drift is weaker, and more variation can be maintained.
Genetic diversity therefore reflects a balance between mutation adding variation and drift removing it.
Now consider deleterious alleles.
Mutation continuously produces harmful mutations, while natural selection removes them.
However, mutation never stops.
As a result, deleterious alleles persist at low frequencies in the population.
Stronger selection keeps these alleles rarer, while higher mutation rates increase their frequency slightly.
The key idea is that mutation maintains genetic variation even when other evolutionary forces remove it.
Without mutation, genetic variation would eventually disappear.

title: Introduction to Population Genetics
text:
Biological and Social Applications


Real-world applications
Population genetics informs:

Conservation biology

Managing genetic diversity

Preventing inbreeding depression

Designing sustainable breeding programs

Medical genetics

Estimating carrier and disease risk

Understanding recessive disorders

Interpreting GWAS findings

Forensic science

Calculating DNA match probabilities

Accounting for population structure



Core principles applied
These applications rely on:

Allele frequencies

Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium

Inbreeding and genetic drift

Linkage disequilibrium

Natural selection

Population genetics connects
DNA variation → population patterns → real-world decisions.


Population genetics is not only theoretical. Its principles are applied widely in biology and society.
In conservation biology, small populations are vulnerable to genetic drift and inbreeding. Genetic analysis helps maintain diversity, reduce inbreeding depression, and design sustainable breeding strategies.
In medical genetics, Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium is used to estimate carrier frequencies for recessive disorders. Mutation–selection balance explains why some disease alleles persist in populations. Linkage disequilibrium forms the foundation of genome-wide association studies.
In forensic science, DNA match probabilities are calculated using allele frequencies and Hardy–Weinberg assumptions. Population structure must be considered carefully to avoid biased probability estimates.
The key message is this:
Population genetics links molecular variation to population-level patterns and ultimately to practical decisions in conservation, medicine, and law.

title: Introduction to Population Genetics
text:
Conservation Genetics


Genetic Risks in Small Populations
When population size declines:

Genetic bottlenecks reduce diversity

Genetic drift removes alleles randomly

Inbreeding increases homozygosity

Recessive deleterious alleles become expressed

Consequences:

Reduced adaptive potential

Increased risk of inbreeding depression
(reduced survival or reproduction)


Management Dilemma
Key question:
Should conservation programs
minimize inbreeding
or allow inbreeding to purge deleterious alleles?

Theoretical argument:

Inbreeding exposes harmful alleles

Selection may remove some of them (“purging”)

Empirical evidence:

Inbreeding often reduces fitness

Maintaining genetic diversity is generally safer



Conservation genetics examines the genetic consequences of small population size.
When populations decline sharply, genetic bottlenecks reduce variation in a single generation.
Genetic drift becomes stronger, randomly eliminating alleles.
In small populations, individuals are also more likely to mate with relatives, increasing inbreeding.
Inbreeding increases homozygosity across the genome.
As homozygosity rises, recessive deleterious alleles are more likely to be expressed.
This can lead to inbreeding depression, which means reduced survival, reduced fertility, or both.
A long-standing debate concerns purging.
The theoretical idea is that inbreeding exposes harmful alleles, allowing natural selection to remove them from the population.
In principle, this could reduce genetic load over time.
However, empirical studies show that inbreeding more often reduces population fitness than successfully eliminates deleterious alleles.
For this reason, most conservation strategies aim to:
Increase effective population size, maintain gene flow between populations, and preserve genetic diversity.
The central objective is to maintain long-term evolutionary potential.

title: Introduction to Population Genetics
text:
Population Genetics in Medicine


Why Allele Frequencies Matter
Population genetics allows us to:

Estimate carrier frequencies
Calculate disease risk
Predict the impact of inbreeding
Interpret population screening data

Using Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium:

Genotype frequencies can be inferred
from allele frequencies
Carrier frequencies can be estimated
without pedigrees


Example: Recessive Disease
Under Hardy–Weinberg:

Disease frequency = \(q^2\)
Allele frequency = \(q = \sqrt{q^2}\)
Carrier frequency = \(2pq\)

Effect of inbreeding:
\[
\text{Homozygote frequency} = q^2 + Fpq
\]

\(F\) = inbreeding coefficient

Inbreeding increases homozygosity

Recessive disease risk increases



Population genetics allows us to estimate disease risk at the population level, even without detailed family pedigrees.
Consider a recessive disorder.
Under Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of affected individuals equals q squared.
If we observe the disease frequency, we can calculate the allele frequency q by taking the square root.
Once we know q, we can compute the carrier frequency.
Under Hardy–Weinberg, the carrier frequency equals 2 p q.
These calculations are widely used in genetic counseling and population screening programs.
Now consider inbreeding.
Inbreeding increases the probability that two alleles are identical by descent.
Under inbreeding, the homozygote frequency becomes
q squared plus F p q.
The additional term, F p q, represents the excess homozygotes caused by inbreeding.
This explains why consanguineous marriages increase the risk of recessive disorders.
The key point is:
Population genetic theory provides a quantitative framework for estimating medical risk.

title: Introduction to Population Genetics
text:
DNA Forensics


Genetic Basis of Forensic Analysis
DNA identification relies on:

Microsatellite markers (STRs)
Highly polymorphic, multi-allelic loci
Population allele frequencies
Estimated from reference databases
Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
Used to calculate genotype probabilities

Multiple independent loci are analyzed
to increase discriminatory power.

Statistical Interpretation
We evaluate the random match probability:
\[
P(\text{match} \mid \text{unrelated individual})
\]
This is the probability that a random person
would share the same DNA profile.

Assuming independence across loci:

Genotype probabilities are multiplied

Overall probability becomes extremely small

Very small probability → strong statistical evidence


DNA evidence does not prove guilt directly. It provides statistical evidence.
Forensic analysis typically uses short tandem repeats, or STR markers.
STRs are highly polymorphic, meaning they have many alleles. This makes them highly informative for distinguishing individuals.
To evaluate a match, we use population allele frequency databases.
Under Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, we calculate genotype probabilities at each locus.
For heterozygotes, the probability equals 2 p q. For homozygotes, it equals p squared.
Assuming loci are independent — that is, in linkage equilibrium — we multiply probabilities across loci.
This produces the random match probability:
The probability that a random, unrelated individual would share the same DNA profile.
With many STR markers, this probability can become extremely small — often one in millions or billions.
Population genetics therefore converts a DNA match into a quantitative statistical statement.
The reliability of this statement depends on:
Accurate allele frequency estimates, appropriate population reference data, and correct assumptions about independence.

title: Introduction to Population Genetics
text:
Summary Population Genetics


What We Observe

DNA sequence variation

Allele and genotype frequencies

Linkage disequilibrium

Population differences

Represent measurable genetic patterns.

The Null Model
Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium

Random mating

Infinite population (no drift)

No mutation, migration, or selection

Deviations indicate evolutionary forces.






Evolutionary Forces

Mutation

Migration (gene flow)

Recombination

Genetic drift

Natural selection

Change in allele frequencies over time




What These Forces Shape

Genetic diversity

Population structure

Linkage disequilibrium

Genomic signatures of history

Medicine, conservation, and forensics

Population genetics connects patterns → processes → consequences


This slide summarizes the entire chapter within a single conceptual framework.
Start in the upper left.
Population genetics begins with observable patterns: DNA variation, allele frequencies, genotype distributions, linkage disequilibrium, and differences between populations.
These are measurable quantities.
However, patterns alone do not explain themselves.
That is where the null model comes in.
Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium defines what we expect in the absence of evolutionary forces.
If mating is random, the population is infinitely large, and no mutation, migration, or selection occurs, allele frequencies remain constant.
This defines no evolutionary change.
When real populations deviate from this expectation, we infer that evolutionary forces are operating.
Those forces are listed in the lower left panel.
Mutation introduces new alleles. Migration moves alleles between populations. Recombination reshuffles alleles. Genetic drift changes frequencies randomly in finite populations. Natural selection changes them non-randomly.
In population genetics, evolution has a precise definition: a change in allele frequencies across generations.
Finally, the lower right panel shows what these forces shape.
They determine levels of genetic diversity, the structure of populations, patterns of linkage disequilibrium, and the genomic signatures of past events.
They also inform applications in medicine, conservation biology, and forensic science.
The central idea of this chapter is:
Population genetics explains why genetic patterns look the way they do, by connecting observable variation to the evolutionary processes that shape it.
That is the framework of the field.

1. From two alleles to one dosage
At a diploid biallelic locus, each individual has two allele copies. Suppose the labels are A and B, and we choose A as the counted allele.

A count of zero is an observed BB genotype. NA means the genotype is unknown. A and B name alleles; they do not establish dominance, causal effects or which allele is rarer.
Question 1. Can a value of 1 identify which parent transmitted A?






Suggested answer





No. A dosage of 1 describes a heterozygote. It carries no parental-origin information. At multiple loci, dosages also do not establish which alleles occur on the same chromosome.

title: Understanding genotype data

2. Read a small genotype matrix
Rows identify individuals and columns identify loci. At L1, dosage counts A; at L2, dosage counts C. These are hypothetical marker labels, not physical genome positions.


Show R code

           L2 = c(0L, 1L, 2L, 2L, NA_integer_, 1L))

                      counted_allele=c("A", "C"),
                      other_allele=c("B", "D"))

          identical(colnames(M), markers$marker),
          all(M[!is.na(M)] %in% 0:2))

Figure 1: Called dosages at two hypothetical loci. Gray cells are missing calls; the counted allele differs between columns.





This practical uses called integer genotypes. Fractional dosages can represent expected allele counts from imputation; they do not identify hard genotype classes without a separate calling rule. Polyploid, multiallelic or haploid data also need different contracts.

3. Keep identities and allele metadata aligned
Row positions are not identities. Suppose a phenotype table arrives in another order.


Show R code

                      hypothetical_trait=c(12,10,15))
position <- match(records$individual,rownames(M))
stopifnot(!anyNA(position), !anyDuplicated(records$individual))

Question 3. Why would selecting the first three matrix rows be incorrect here?






Suggested answer





Those rows belong to individuals 1, 2 and 3, not the individuals listed in the records. Equal row counts do not guarantee a correct mapping. Marker metadata must similarly follow columns when they are reordered; physical positions and allele orientation cannot be inferred from matrix dimensions.

text:
4. Reverse the counted allele
For diploid calls, B dosage is \(2-\)A dosage. Missing calls stay missing.


Show R code

B_copies <- 2L-A_copies
comparison <- data.frame(individual=rownames(M), A_copies, B_copies)

individual4 individual4        0        2

          all((A_copies+B_copies)[!is.na(A_copies)]==2))


Question 4. Does changing the counted allele change the underlying individuals or their heterozygosity?






Suggested answer





No. The two homozygote labels exchange roles and heterozygotes remain heterozygotes. The reported counted-allele frequency changes to its complement. Always state the counted allele with a result; numeric dosages alone do not establish allele identity.

title: Understanding genotype data
text:
5. Distinguish genotype from haplotype phase
Individual 2 is heterozygous at both loci. Two possible chromosome pairs are



Phase configuration
Chromosome 1
Chromosome 2




Coupling
A–C
B–D


Repulsion
A–D
B–C



Both produce one A copy and one C copy, so both have the same unphased row (1,1).


Show R code
coupling <- rbind(c("A","C"),c("B","D"))
repulsion <- rbind(c("A","D"),c("B","C"))
counted <- c("A","C")
phase_dosage <- function(chromosomes) {
  vapply(1:2,function(j) sum(chromosomes[,j]==counted[j]),integer(1))
}
rbind(coupling=phase_dosage(coupling), repulsion=phase_dosage(repulsion))


          [,1] [,2]
coupling     1    1
repulsion    1    1


Show R code
stopifnot(identical(phase_dosage(coupling),phase_dosage(repulsion)))


Question 5. Can the matrix tell us whether individual 2 carries the A–C haplotype?






Suggested answer





No. Phase information or a declared inference method is required. Frequencies of unphased allele counts are observed summaries; haplotype frequencies cannot be read directly from those counts. Dosage correlation should not automatically be called haplotype linkage disequilibrium.

1. Count the called genotypes
At our diploid biallelic locus, dosage counts copies of A: 2 means AA, 1 means AB and 0 means BB. The third individual has an unknown genotype.


Show R code
dosage <- c(2L,1L,NA_integer_,0L,1L,2L)
called <- dosage[!is.na(dosage)]
stopifnot(length(called)>0L,all(called %in% 0:2))

Question 1. What is the genotype-frequency denominator? What is the allele-frequency denominator?






Suggested answer





Five called individuals give the genotype denominator. Ten called allele copies give the allele denominator. The missing individual contributes neither a known genotype nor known allele copies. Excluding missing calls describes the called sample; it does not prove missingness is ignorable for population inference.

title: Allele frequencies and Hardy–Weinberg expectations
text:
2. Calculate observed frequencies and heterozygosity
For called counts \(n_{AA},n_{AB},n_{BB}\),
\[\hat p_A=\frac{2n_{AA}+n_{AB}}{2n_c},\qquad
\hat q_B=1-\hat p_A,\qquad H_O=\frac{n_{AB}}{n_c}.\]
No HWE assumption is required for these observed summaries.


Show R code

p_A <- sum(called)/(2*n_called)
q_B <- 1-p_A

Question 2. Is the A frequency 0.6 the same quantity as the AA frequency 0.4?






Suggested answer





No. Allele frequency counts allele copies, while genotype frequency counts individuals. Two AA individuals contribute four A copies, and two AB individuals contribute two more. Observed heterozygosity is the fraction of called individuals with AB, here 0.4.




Allele reversal and all-missing loci

An all-missing locus has no called denominator: its frequency is undefined, not zero. A monomorphic called locus has a defined frequency of zero or one.

title: Allele frequencies and Hardy–Weinberg expectations
text:
3. Derive HWE expectations
Assume two independently sampled gametes from one pool, each carrying A with probability \(p\) and B with probability \(q=1-p\). AA requires A from both gametes, giving \(p^2\). AB has two ordered possibilities, A then B or B then A, giving \(2pq\). BB has probability \(q^2\).
\[f_{AA}=p^2,\qquad f_{AB}=2pq,\qquad f_{BB}=q^2.\]
The proportions sum to \((p+q)^2=1\). This describes genotype formation at supplied frequencies. Stable allele frequencies over generations require additional assumptions about selection, migration, mutation and drift. Random union of gametes does not force a small sample to match its expectations exactly.


Show R code
expected <- c(AA=p_A^2,AB=2*p_A*q_B,BB=q_B^2)
expected_counts <- n_called*expected
H_expected <- unname(expected["AB"])

Suggested answer





Expected counts are averages over possible samples, not a particular realized sample. Here they are 1.8, 2.4 and 0.8. Rounding them would replace the model expectation with arbitrary integers.

Question 4. Why is \(H_E=2p(1-p)\) zero at fixation and maximal at \(p=0.5\)?






Suggested answer





At fixation only one allele is present, so different alleles cannot pair. Since \(2p(1-p)=0.5-2(p-0.5)^2\), its maximum is 0.5 at equal allele frequencies. This describes random pairing; an observed sample or a nonrandom mating system need not have heterozygosity at most 0.5.

Question 5. Does a heterozygote deficit in one sample prove inbreeding?






Suggested answer





No. Finite sampling, population mixtures, relatives, nonrandom mating or genotype errors can affect the comparison. Formal assessment requires a declared sampling model and a suitable test. Expected counts in this five-individual example are too small for an automatic large-sample chi-squared approximation. This practical does not conduct an HWE test or identify a cause of departure.

title: Population structure, mating and inbreeding
text:
1. Specify the mating rule
A parent with genotype AA transmits A with probability 1, AB with probability 0.5, and BB with probability 0. For a specified pair of parents with transmission probabilities \(t_1,t_2\), Mendelian transmission gives
\[P(AA)=t_1t_2,\quad P(AB)=t_1(1-t_2)+(1-t_1)t_2,\quad
P(BB)=(1-t_1)(1-t_2).\]
These are probabilities at one locus. They do not state that a parent’s whole genome is sampled independently at every marker.


Show R code
cross_probabilities <- function(t1,t2) {
  c(AA=t1*t2,AB=t1*(1-t2)+(1-t1)*t2,BB=(1-t1)*(1-t2))
}
crosses <- rbind(AA_by_BB=cross_probabilities(1,0),
                 AB_by_AB=cross_probabilities(.5,.5))
crosses


           AA  AB   BB
AA_by_BB 0.00 1.0 0.00
AB_by_AB 0.25 0.5 0.25


Show R code
stopifnot(identical(unname(crosses["AA_by_BB",]),c(0,1,0)),
          identical(unname(crosses["AB_by_AB",]),c(.25,.5,.25)))


Question 1. Can an offspring population have heterozygosity above 0.5?






Suggested answer





Yes. AA-by-BB crosses produce AB offspring with probability 1. The maximum of 0.5 in \(2pq\) applies to random union of gametes from one common pool, not every mating rule.




Compare random pairing and pairing by genotype
Suppose adult genotype proportions are HWE proportions at \(p_A=0.6\). Under random pairing, pair weights are the products of adult genotype frequencies. Under a hypothetical same-genotype rule, AA pairs only with AA, AB with AB, and BB with BB. Each genotype contributes parents in proportion to its adult frequency, and every pair has equal reproductive output.


Show R code
p <- 0.6
q <- 1-p
adult <- c(AA=p^2,AB=2*p*q,BB=q^2)
transmission <- c(AA=1,AB=.5,BB=0)
random_pairs <- outer(adult,adult)
same_genotype_pairs <- diag(adult)
# Pair weights sum to one; rows/columns refer to the two parental roles.
offspring_expectation <- function(pair_weights) {
  stopifnot(all(pair_weights >= 0),abs(sum(pair_weights)-1)<1e-12)
  result <- c(AA=0,AB=0,BB=0)
  for(i in 1:3) for(j in 1:3) {
    result <- result + pair_weights[i,j]*
      cross_probabilities(unname(transmission[i]),unname(transmission[j]))
  }
  result
}
random_offspring <- offspring_expectation(random_pairs)
assortative_offspring <- offspring_expectation(same_genotype_pairs)

Question 2. Which quantity changes under the same-genotype rule: genotype proportions or allele frequency?






Suggested answer





Genotype proportions change: heterozygosity falls from 0.48 to 0.24. A frequency remains 0.6 because parental allele contributions are unchanged. Unequal reproductive output or genotype-dependent selection could change it. This example specifies mating by genotype, not genealogical relatedness; its heterozygote deficit does not establish identity by descent.

title: Population structure, mating and inbreeding
text:
2. Distinguish state from descent
Two A copies are identical by state because they have the same allele label. They are identical by descent (IBD) relative to a specified ancestral base if they descend from the same ancestral allele copy. A homozygous AA genotype alone does not identify which history produced it.
For an individual, pedigree inbreeding \(F\) is the probability that its two allele copies at a locus are IBD under the pedigree and founder assumptions. The additive relationship diagonal is \(A_{ii}=1+F_i\); parental kinship is \(A_{sd}/2\).

A small pedigree calculation
Take two unrelated, noninbred founders, each with two distinct ancestral allele-copy identities. Two of their offspring are full siblings. If those siblings mate, their offspring can receive the same ancestral copy through both parents.
For either sibling’s transmitted copy, each of the four founder copies has probability 1/4 under Mendelian transmission. Averaging over the siblings’ inheritance and transmissions, the probability of a match is \(4(1/4)^2=1/4\).


Show R code
founder_copies <- c("sire_copy1","sire_copy2","dam_copy1","dam_copy2")
transmitted_copy_probability <- setNames(rep(.25,4),founder_copies)
F_fullsib_offspring <- sum(transmitted_copy_probability^2)
c(F=F_fullsib_offspring,relationship_diagonal=1+F_fullsib_offspring)

                 0.25                  1.25 


Show R code
stopifnot(F_fullsib_offspring==.25)


This is an expectation from a declared pedigree, not the fraction of homozygous genotypes observed in one individual. Founders are assumed unrelated and noninbred relative to this base; changing the base or assumptions changes the interpretation.

title: Population structure, mating and inbreeding
text:
3. Derive the inbreeding genotype model
Let A have frequency \(p\) and B frequency \(q=1-p\) in the reference pool. In the simple model, with probability \(F\) both copies are IBD and share one ancestral draw; with probability \(1-F\) they are independent draws from that pool. Then
\[f_{AA}=Fp+(1-F)p^2=p^2+Fpq,\] \[f_{AB}=2pq(1-F),\qquad f_{BB}=q^2+Fpq.\]
IBD pairs contribute no heterozygotes. Relative to HWE, each homozygote increases by \(Fpq\), and AB decreases by \(2Fpq\). This model preserves the supplied allele frequency; it is not a complete model of drift, selection or a multigeneration breeding programme.


Show R code
inbreeding_proportions <- function(p,F) {
  stopifnot(length(p)==1L,length(F)==1L,is.finite(p),is.finite(F),
            p>=0,p<=1,F>=0,F<=1)
  q <- 1-p
  c(AA=p^2+F*p*q,AB=2*p*q*(1-F),BB=q^2+F*p*q)
}
F_values <- c(0,.25,1)
model <- t(vapply(F_values,function(F) inbreeding_proportions(.6,F),numeric(3)))
rownames(model) <- paste0("F=",F_values)

Question 3. Why does complete homozygosity not imply that A is fixed?






Suggested answer





At \(F=1\), the model gives AA proportion \(p\) and BB proportion \(q\), with no heterozygotes. Both alleles can remain present in different individuals. Homozygosity describes how copies are paired; fixation describes absence of an allele from the population.

This is the Wahlund effect: pooling populations creates a heterozygote deficit relative to HWE at the pooled frequency, even when each population follows its own HWE expectation.
For weights \(w_k\) summing to one, \(\bar p=\sum_k w_kp_k\). The difference is
\[2\bar p(1-\bar p)-\sum_k w_k2p_k(1-p_k)
=2\sum_k w_k(p_k-\bar p)^2.\]
It is twice the weighted variance of population allele frequencies. In this toy example the pooled heterozygosity is 0.18, while the pooled HWE expectation is 0.5.

title: Measuring genetic diversity
text:
1. Observed heterozygosity and gene diversity
At a diploid biallelic locus, observed heterozygosity \(H_O\) is the fraction of called individuals that are heterozygous. Gene diversity is
\[H_E=1-\sum_k p_k^2=2p(1-p)\]
for two alleles. It is the probability that two independent allele draws from the specified frequency pool differ. It is an expected genotype heterozygosity only under the appropriate random-union model. Calculating this frequency summary does not establish HWE.


Show R code
dosage <- c(2L,1L,NA_integer_,0L,1L,2L) # Counts A.
called <- dosage[!is.na(dosage)]
stopifnot(all(called %in% 0:2),length(called)>0L)
n_individuals <- length(called)
n_alleles <- 2*n_individuals
p <- sum(called)/n_alleles
HO <- mean(called==1L)
HE <- 2*p*(1-p)
c(called_individuals=n_individuals,called_alleles=n_alleles,
  p_A=p,observed_heterozygosity=HO,gene_diversity=HE)


     called_individuals          called_alleles                     p_A 
                   5.00                   10.00                    0.60 
observed_heterozygosity          gene_diversity 
                   0.40                    0.48 


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(HO-.4)<1e-12,abs(HE-.48)<1e-12)


Question 1. Why are 0.4 and 0.48 different, and which is a direct description of heterozygous individuals?






Suggested answer





\(H_O=0.4\) directly describes called genotypes. \(H_E=0.48\) describes independent pairing at the estimated allele frequencies. Their difference can reflect finite sampling, mating, structure or other processes; it does not by itself identify a biological cause.

title: Measuring genetic diversity
text:
2. A finite-sample correction
Suppose \(m\) allele copies are sampled independently from a fixed population frequency distribution. The plug-in diversity \(1-\sum_k\hat p_k^2\) is downward biased because a finite sample estimates its own frequencies. The corrected estimator is
\[\widehat H_{unbiased}=\frac{m}{m-1}\left(1-\sum_k\hat p_k^2\right),\qquad m>1.\]
It is also the fraction of distinct sampled-copy pairs carrying different alleles. Its population-unbiased interpretation requires independent, identically distributed allele-copy sampling; counting two copies per diploid individual does not automatically establish independence. Relatives, inbreeding, population mixtures and informative missingness require an appropriate sampling treatment.


Show R code
corrected_HE <- n_alleles/(n_alleles-1)*HE
# Reconstruct the allele-copy labels only for this one-locus count example.
allele_copies <- c(rep("A",sum(called)),rep("B",n_alleles-sum(called)))
copy_pairs <- combn(seq_along(allele_copies),2)
pair_difference <- mean(allele_copies[copy_pairs[1,]] !=
                        allele_copies[copy_pairs[2,]])
c(plugin=HE,corrected=corrected_HE,distinct_copy_pair_fraction=pair_difference)


                     plugin                   corrected 
                  0.4800000                   0.5333333 
distinct_copy_pair_fraction 
                  0.5333333 


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(corrected_HE-pair_difference)<1e-12)


The corrected result is about 0.533. It can exceed the population-model maximum of 0.5 in a small biallelic sample; do not silently truncate it. A correction for bias is not a confidence interval, nor a correction for related sampling.

Verify the bias by exact enumeration
Take four independent allele draws from a known population with \(p_A=0.6\). Enumerate all 16 ordered outcomes rather than simulate a large experiment.


Show R code
outcomes <- as.matrix(expand.grid(rep(list(0:1),4)))
m <- ncol(outcomes)
p_true <- .6
A_count <- rowSums(outcomes)
probability <- p_true^A_count*(1-p_true)^(m-A_count)
p_sample <- A_count/m
plugin_values <- 2*p_sample*(1-p_sample)
corrected_values <- m/(m-1)*plugin_values
expectations <- c(population_diversity=2*p_true*(1-p_true),
  expected_plugin=sum(probability*plugin_values),
  expected_corrected=sum(probability*corrected_values))
expectations


population_diversity      expected_plugin   expected_corrected 
                0.48                 0.36                 0.48

          abs(expectations["expected_plugin"]-.36)<1e-12,
          abs(expectations["expected_corrected"]-.48)<1e-12)


Question 2. Does the correction make every observed sample equal to the true diversity?






Suggested answer





No. It corrects the average over repeated samples under the declared model, not the error in each sample. A monomorphic four-copy sample still has estimated diversity zero even though the population is polymorphic.

Question 3. Why does averaging only polymorphic loci give a higher value?

Question 4. Why are nucleotide diversity and whole-haplotype diversity different?

title: Mutation, migration and linkage disequilibrium
text:
1. Mutation changes allele frequencies
At one biallelic locus, let A have frequency \(p\). Suppose A changes to a with probability \(u\), and a changes to A with probability \(v\) per generation. Then
\[p'=p(1-u)+(1-p)v,\qquad \Delta p=v(1-p)-up.\]
The first term retains A copies; the second gains A through reverse mutation. This two-state model does not represent all possible nucleotide substitutions or multiallelic mutation.


Show R code
mutation_step <- function(p,u,v) {
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(c(p,u,v))),all(c(p,u,v)>=0),all(c(p,u,v)<=1))
  p*(1-u)+(1-p)*v
}
mutation_step(.3,.1,.2)


[1] 0.41


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(mutation_step(.3,.1,.2)-.41)<1e-12,
          mutation_step(.3,0,0)==.3,
          mutation_step(1,.1,0)==.9)


Question 1. If both mutation directions operate, what balances at equilibrium?






Suggested answer





Loss \(up\) equals gain \(v(1-p)\). For \(u+v>0\), the fixed point is \(p^*=v/(u+v)\). Its approach depends on the recursion factor \(1-u-v\). For the illustrative small rates below, this factor lies between zero and one and the trajectory approaches the fixed point monotonically.





Show R code
u <- .02
v <- .01
steps <- 100L
p_mutation <- numeric(steps+1L)
p_mutation[1] <- .8
for(t in seq_len(steps)) p_mutation[t+1L] <- mutation_step(p_mutation[t],u,v)
p_equilibrium <- v/(u+v)
closed_form <- p_equilibrium+(.8-p_equilibrium)*(1-u-v)^(0:steps)
stopifnot(max(abs(p_mutation-closed_form))<1e-12)
plot(0:steps,p_mutation,type="l",lwd=2,col="#247BA0",ylim=c(0,1),
     xlab="Generation",ylab="A frequency")
abline(h=p_equilibrium,lty=2,col="#B65C39")








Figure 1: A deterministic mutation trajectory at illustrative rates, with the equilibrium frequency shown by a dashed line.





Mutation supplies allele changes; the deterministic trajectory does not describe the fate of an individual new mutation in a finite population.

title: Mutation, migration and linkage disequilibrium
text:
2. Migration changes the reference pool
Let a fraction \(m\) of allele copies in the next pool come from a migrant source with A frequency \(p_M\). The remainder comes from a resident pool with frequency \(p\):
\[p'=(1-m)p+mp_M.\]
Here \(m\) is the gene-pool contribution, not automatically the fraction of individuals moving. We specify the donor frequency at the migration step and assume equal allele-copy weighting within each pool.


Show R code
migration_step <- function(p,p_migrant,m) {
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(c(p,p_migrant,m))),
            all(c(p,p_migrant,m)>=0),all(c(p,p_migrant,m)<=1))
  (1-m)*p+m*p_migrant
}
migration_step(.2,.8,.25)


[1] 0.35


Show R code

          migration_step(.2,.8,0)==.2,
          migration_step(.2,.8,1)==.8)


Question 2. Under repeated migration from a fixed donor, what happens to the difference between resident and donor frequencies?






Suggested answer





The difference is multiplied by \(1-m\) at every step. For \(0<m\leq1\), this simple replacement model approaches the donor frequency. Bidirectional migration, selection or a changing donor require a different recursion.

title: Mutation, migration and linkage disequilibrium
section: 3. Use phased haplotype frequencies for LD
text:
3. Use phased haplotype frequencies for LD
At two loci A/a and B/b, suppose the haplotypes are known. This is a supplied frequency model; it is not phase inferred from unphased dosages.


Show R code
haplotypes <- c(AB=.4,Ab=.1,aB=.1,ab=.4)
ld_summary <- function(h) {
  stopifnot(identical(names(h),c("AB","Ab","aB","ab")),
            all(is.finite(h)),all(h>=0),abs(sum(h)-1)<1e-12)
  pA <- unname(h["AB"]+h["Ab"])
  pB <- unname(h["AB"]+h["aB"])
  D <- unname(h["AB"])-pA*pB
  denominator <- pA*(1-pA)*pB*(1-pB)
  c(p_A=pA,p_B=pB,D=D,
    r_squared=if(denominator>0) D^2/denominator else NA_real_)
}
ld_summary(haplotypes)


      p_A       p_B         D r_squared 
     0.50      0.50      0.15      0.36 


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(ld_summary(haplotypes)["D"]-.15)<1e-12,
          abs(ld_summary(haplotypes)["r_squared"]-.36)<1e-12)


The allele frequencies are the margins of the haplotype table. Define
\[D=f_{AB}-p_Ap_B,\qquad
r^2=\frac{D^2}{p_A(1-p_A)p_B(1-p_B)}.\]
\(r^2\) is defined here only when both loci are polymorphic. \(D\) changes sign if one allele coding is reversed; \(r^2\) does not. The physical linkage of two loci and their statistical association are different concepts. Association can also arise through population structure or other processes.
Question 3. Why can allele frequencies of 0.5 at both loci fail to identify the AB haplotype frequency?






Suggested answer





The margins leave the joint association unspecified. Under independence AB has frequency 0.25; our supplied table gives 0.4. Many different haplotype tables share the same margins. Unphased genotype dosages contain still less direct information about chromosome pairing.

title: Mutation, migration and linkage disequilibrium
section: 4. Recombination reduces LD under a specified model
text:
4. Recombination reduces LD under a specified model
For random mating, no selection, migration, mutation or drift, and recombination fraction \(r\) between the loci, the gametic recursion is
\[f'_{AB}=f_{AB}-rD,\quad f'_{Ab}=f_{Ab}+rD,\] \[f'_{aB}=f_{aB}+rD,\quad f'_{ab}=f_{ab}-rD.\]
Allele frequencies are conserved and \(D'=(1-r)D\). The recombination fraction lies between zero and 0.5 in this two-locus model; it is not a physical distance in base pairs.


Show R code
recombination_step <- function(h,r) {
  stopifnot(length(r)==1L,is.finite(r),r>=0,r<=.5)
  D <- unname(ld_summary(h)["D"])
  next_h <- h+r*D*c(-1,1,1,-1)
  stopifnot(all(next_h>=-1e-12),abs(sum(next_h)-1)<1e-12)
  next_h
}
next_h <- recombination_step(haplotypes,.1)
rbind(Current=haplotypes,Next=next_h)

                  ld_summary(haplotypes)[c("p_A","p_B")]))<1e-12,
          abs(ld_summary(next_h)["D"]-.9*.15)<1e-12)

Question 4. Do unlinked loci (\(r=0.5\)) lose all LD in one generation?






Suggested answer





No. Existing gametic LD is halved under this recursion. Independence is approached over generations when no other process creates association. A larger physical separation does not by itself establish that a sampled population is in linkage equilibrium.

title: Genetic drift in finite populations
text:
1. Define a neutral Wright–Fisher model
Take a fixed population of \(N\) diploid individuals, hence \(2N\) allele copies. Generations do not overlap. The next generation’s copies are sampled independently with replacement from a neutral parental pool at A frequency \(p_t\):
\[K_{t+1}\mid p_t\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(2N,p_t),\qquad
p_{t+1}=K_{t+1}/(2N).\]
There is no mutation, migration or selection. This single-locus model does not generate chromosome inheritance, pedigrees, sex roles or individual phenotypes. It is an allele-count sampling model, not a complete breeding population.
Its conditional moments are
\[E(p_{t+1}\mid p_t)=p_t,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(p_{t+1}\mid p_t)=\frac{p_t(1-p_t)}{2N}.\]
Neutrality preserves the expected frequency, while finite realizations fluctuate.

title: Genetic drift in finite populations
text:
3. Compare population sizes


Show R code
neutral_trajectory <- function(N,p0,generations) {
  stopifnot(length(N)==1L,N>=1,N==as.integer(N),
            length(p0)==1L,is.finite(p0),p0>=0,p0<=1,
            generations>=0,generations==as.integer(generations))
  p <- numeric(generations+1L)
  p[1] <- p0
  for(t in seq_len(generations)) p[t+1L] <- rbinom(1,2*N,p[t])/(2*N)
  p
}
set.seed(20261008)
generations <- 60L
replicates <- 20L
sizes <- c(25L,250L)
trajectories <- lapply(sizes,function(N) {
  replicate(replicates,neutral_trajectory(N,.5,generations))
})
stopifnot(all(vapply(trajectories,function(z) all(z>=0 & z<=1),logical(1))))

Question 2. Why do smaller populations fluctuate more strongly? Is the average of these 20 runs guaranteed to equal 0.5 at every step?






Suggested answer





The conditional variance scales as \(1/(2N)\). A finite average of simulated trajectories also has sampling variation, so it is not guaranteed to equal the theoretical expectation. The two panels are illustrations of that model, not evidence about a real population’s demographic history.

title: Genetic drift in finite populations
text:
4. Track gene diversity
For the random-union diversity \(H_t=2p_t(1-p_t)\),
\[E(H_{t+1}\mid p_t)=\left(1-\frac{1}{2N}\right)H_t,\]
so, from a fixed initial frequency,
\[E(H_t)=H_0\left(1-\frac{1}{2N}\right)^t.\]
This is frequency-based gene diversity, not the observed heterozygote fraction of individually simulated genotypes.

Suggested answer

5. Interpret fixation and loss
Without mutation or migration, frequencies 0 and 1 are absorbing. For this finite neutral model, eventual fixation probability of A is its initial frequency. Reaching fixation by a specified short horizon is a different quantity; runs still segregating at that horizon must not be counted as losses.

In this ideal model \(N\) specifies the sampling variance. A real population’s census size need not equal the effective size governing drift. Unequal reproductive success, sex ratios, overlapping generations and demographic changes can alter the relevant effective size. Its estimation needs a named method and sampling assumptions; these toy trajectories do not estimate it.

title: Selection, fitness and dominance
text:
1. State the life cycle
Begin with random union of gametes at A frequency \(p\), giving zygote proportions \(p^2,2pq,q^2\). Apply genotype fitness weights \(w_{AA},w_{Aa},w_{aa}\) to their reproductive contributions. Count A in the selected pool, then form the next zygotes by random mating. There is no mutation or migration.
\[\bar w=p^2w_{AA}+2pqw_{Aa}+q^2w_{aa},\] \[p'=\frac{p^2w_{AA}+pqw_{Aa}}{\bar w}.\]
Weights describe relative contribution under this model. If the mean contribution is zero, a next-generation pool is undefined. Multiplying every fitness by the same positive constant leaves the allele-frequency recursion unchanged.


Show R code
selection_step <- function(p,fitness) {
  stopifnot(length(p)==1L,is.finite(p),p>=0,p<=1,
            identical(names(fitness),c("AA","Aa","aa")),
            all(is.finite(fitness)),all(fitness>=0))
  zygotes <- c(AA=p^2,Aa=2*p*(1-p),aa=(1-p)^2)
  contribution <- zygotes*fitness
  mean_fitness <- sum(contribution)
  stopifnot(mean_fitness>0)
  selected <- contribution/mean_fitness
  list(p_next=unname(selected["AA"]+selected["Aa"]/2),
       mean_fitness=mean_fitness,zygotes=zygotes,selected=selected)
}
fitness <- c(AA=1.2,Aa=1.1,aa=1)

Question 1. Are the selected contribution proportions automatically HWE proportions at the new frequency?






Suggested answer





No. Genotype-dependent weighting changes the selected pool’s proportions. Random union of its gametes gives HWE expectations for the next zygote stage. The stage at which frequencies are defined matters; selection can recur after that stage.

title: Selection, fitness and dominance
text:
2. Compare fitness dominance
For a beneficial A allele, define \(w_{AA}=1+s\), \(w_{Aa}=1+hs\), \(w_{aa}=1\). Here \(s>0\) is its homozygote advantage and \(h\) specifies heterozygote fitness: 0 recessive, 0.5 intermediate, and 1 dominant in this parameterization.


Show R code
selection_trajectory <- function(p0,fitness,generations) {
  p <- numeric(generations+1L)
  p[1] <- p0
  for(t in seq_len(generations)) p[t+1L] <- selection_step(p[t],fitness)$p_next
  p
}
s <- .2
h_values <- c(Recessive=0,Intermediate=.5,Dominant=1)
fitness_models <- lapply(h_values,function(h) c(AA=1+s,Aa=1+h*s,aa=1))

                       numeric(81))

Question 2. Why can a rare beneficial recessive allele increase slowly?






Suggested answer





Most of its copies occur in heterozygotes when it is rare. Under the recessive fitness model those heterozygotes have no advantage, and advantageous AA homozygotes are uncommon. Conversely, near fixation a dominant beneficial allele can leave the alternative allele hidden in equally fit heterozygotes, slowing its removal.

title: Selection, fitness and dominance
section: 3. Heterozygote advantage can maintain a polymorphism
text:
3. Heterozygote advantage can maintain a polymorphism
Suppose \(w_{AA}=1-s\), \(w_{Aa}=1\), \(w_{aa}=1-t\), with \(s,t>0\). The interior equilibrium is
\[p^*=\frac{t}{s+t}.\]
Both alleles can increase when rare because heterozygotes exceed either homozygote in fitness. This is one explicit balancing-selection model, not a claim that every polymorphism is maintained by selection.

Question 3. Does this deterministic equilibrium guarantee that both alleles persist in a finite population?






Suggested answer





No. Drift can still reach loss or fixation. Balancing selection changes the transition probabilities but does not create a missing allele when mutation and migration are absent. The deterministic model and finite-population model answer different questions.

title: Selection, fitness and dominance
section: 4. Combine selection with finite allele-copy sampling
text:
4. Combine selection with finite allele-copy sampling
Use the selected-pool frequency as the probability of sampling \(2N\) copies for the next generation:
\[K_{t+1}\mid p_t\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(2N,p_{selected}(p_t)).\]
This is a specified one-locus selection-plus-drift model. It does not simulate sex-specific mating, individual family sizes, chromosome recombination or breeding programme constraints.


Show R code
selected_drift_trajectory <- function(N,p0,fitness,generations) {
  stopifnot(N>=1,N==as.integer(N),generations>=0,
            generations==as.integer(generations))
  p <- numeric(generations+1L)
  p[1] <- p0
  for(t in seq_len(generations)) {
    p_selected <- selection_step(p[t],fitness)$p_next
    p[t+1L] <- rbinom(1,2*N,p_selected)/(2*N)
  }
  p
}

title: Testing Hardy–Weinberg proportions
section: 1. State the sampling model and null hypothesis
text:
1. State the sampling model and null hypothesis
We study one diploid biallelic autosomal locus with accurately called AA, AB and BB genotypes. The sample consists of independent individuals from a declared population, without outcome-dependent ascertainment. Missing calls are excluded and their denominator reported. Relatives, pooled populations, uncertain genotype calls or sex-linked inheritance require a different model or analysis.
The null is that genotype probabilities follow \(p_A^2,2p_A(1-p_A),(1-p_A)^2\) for some population allele frequency. A test compares counts with this model; it does not test every mechanism associated with random mating or identify why a departure occurred.


Show R code
validate_counts <- function(counts) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(counts),length(counts)==3,!is.null(names(counts)),
    !anyDuplicated(names(counts)),setequal(names(counts),c("AA","AB","BB")),
    all(is.finite(counts)),all(counts>=0),all(counts==floor(counts)),
    sum(counts)>0,sum(counts)<=1000)
  counts[c("AA","AB","BB")]
}
hwe_summary <- function(counts) {
  counts <- validate_counts(counts)
  n <- sum(counts)
  pA <- (2*counts["AA"]+counts["AB"])/(2*n)
  expected <- n*c(AA=unname(pA)^2,AB=2*unname(pA)*(1-unname(pA)),
                   BB=(1-unname(pA))^2)
  list(counts=counts,n=n,pA=unname(pA),expected=expected)
}

stopifnot(s$n==100,abs(s$pA-.66)<1e-12,
          max(abs(s$expected-c(43.56,44.88,11.56)))<1e-12)

title: Testing Hardy–Weinberg proportions
text:
2. Calculate a chi-square approximation
For positive fitted expectations,
\[X^2=\sum_{g\in\{AA,AB,BB\}}\frac{(O_g-E_g)^2}{E_g}.\]
Three category counts have two free proportions because they sum to the sample size. Estimating one allele-frequency parameter from the same sample leaves \(3-1-1=1\) degree of freedom. This is an asymptotic approximation, particularly questionable when an expected genotype count is small.


Show R code
hwe_chisq <- function(counts) {
  s <- hwe_summary(counts)
  if(any(s$expected==0)) {
    return(c(statistic=NA_real_,df=NA_real_,p_value=NA_real_))
  }
  statistic <- sum((s$counts-s$expected)^2/s$expected)
  c(statistic=unname(statistic),df=1,
    p_value=pchisq(statistic,df=1,lower.tail=FALSE))
}

The generic call gives the same statistic but uses two degrees of freedom, because it does not know that those probabilities were fitted from these counts. Its default p-value therefore does not implement this fitted HWE test. No continuity correction is used in our calculation.
Question 1. What if allele frequency were genuinely specified before sampling?






Suggested answer





Then the three genotype probabilities would be fully specified, with two degrees of freedom in a regular goodness-of-fit approximation. That tests a particular allele frequency as well as HWE proportions. It is a different null from fitting allele frequency within the current sample.

title: Testing Hardy–Weinberg proportions
text:
3. Enumerate an exact conditional distribution
Condition on sample size \(n\) and the observed number \(K\) of B copies. For a possible heterozygote count \(h\),
\[n_{BB}=(K-h)/2,\qquad n_{AA}=n-h-n_{BB}.\]
Only nonnegative integer configurations are allowed. Under the independent-individual HWE model, their conditional probabilities are
\[P(h\mid n,K)=
\frac{n!\,2^h}{n_{AA}!\,h!\,n_{BB}!\,\binom{2n}{K}}.\]
The factor \(2^h\) accounts for the two orders of unlike alleles in each heterozygote. Conditioning removes the unknown allele-frequency parameter. We define a probability-ordered two-sided p-value as the sum of probabilities of configurations no more probable than the observed configuration, including ties. This is not a mid-p test or a doubled one-sided tail. For exact-test conventions and efficient algorithms, see Wigginton, Cutler and Abecasis (2005).


Show R code
hwe_exact <- function(counts) {
  counts <- validate_counts(counts)
  n <- sum(counts); K <- unname(counts["AB"]+2*counts["BB"])
  h <- seq.int(K %% 2,min(K,2*n-K),by=2)
  BB <- (K-h)/2; AA <- n-h-BB
  log_probability <- lgamma(n+1)+h*log(2)-lgamma(AA+1)-
    lgamma(h+1)-lgamma(BB+1)-lchoose(2*n,K)
  probability <- exp(log_probability)
  stopifnot(abs(sum(probability)-1)<1e-10)
  probability <- probability/sum(probability) # Floating-point normalization.
  observed <- match(unname(counts["AB"]),h)
  included <- log_probability<=log_probability[observed]+1e-10
  p_value <- min(1,sum(probability[included]))
  list(p_value=p_value,n=n,B_copies=K,
       distribution=data.frame(AA=AA,AB=h,BB=BB,probability=probability,
                               included_in_p_value=included))
}

title: Testing Hardy–Weinberg proportions
section: 5. Interpret a departure without naming its cause
text:
5. Interpret a departure without naming its cause
Population structure, nonrandom mating, selection or technical calling errors can produce departures from the tested proportions. Which mechanism applies needs additional information. Sampling relatives can also invalidate the independent-individual null distribution even when marginal genotype proportions match.
A hypothetical population mixture has two equal groups with HWE counts corresponding to allele frequencies 0.9 and 0.1. Within-group counts fit their models exactly, but pooled counts do not fit the random-union model at frequency 0.5.

Report the population and locus definitions, called sample size, genotype counts, missingness, relatedness/ascertainment rules, test convention and threshold. A threshold alone is not a universal reason to discard every departing locus.

title: Mutation, selection and drift at balance
text:
1. Define the mutation–selection life cycle
Let \(q\) be the frequency of a deleterious allele a among zygotes, with \(p=1-q\). Random union gives AA, Aa and aa proportions \(p^2,2pq,q^2\). Their fitness weights are \(1,1-hs,1-s\), where \(s\) is the aa disadvantage and \(h\) specifies its expression in heterozygotes.
First apply selection. The a frequency in selected contributions is
\[q_s=\frac{q^2(1-s)+pq(1-hs)}
{p^2+2pq(1-hs)+q^2(1-s)}.\]
Then mutate A to a at rate \(u\), without reverse mutation:
\[q'=q_s+u(1-q_s).\]
The next generation starts with random union at \(q'\). This model is deterministic, with no drift or migration. Complete recessivity is \(h=0\); \(h=0.5\) gives an intermediate fitness disadvantage. These are fitness effects, not necessarily dominance for a measured trait.


Show R code
selection_frequency <- function(q,s,h) {
  stopifnot(length(q)==1,is.finite(q),q>=0,q<=1,
            length(s)==1,is.finite(s),s>=0,s<1,
            length(h)==1,is.finite(h),h>=0,h<=1)
  p <- 1-q
  w <- p^2+2*p*q*(1-h*s)+q^2*(1-s)
  (q^2*(1-s)+p*q*(1-h*s))/w
}
balance_step <- function(q,u,s,h) {
  stopifnot(length(u)==1,is.finite(u),u>=0,u<1)
  selected <- selection_frequency(q,s,h)
  selected+u*(1-selected)
}
u <- 1e-4; s <- .1
stopifnot(abs(balance_step(.3,0,0,.5)-.3)<1e-12,
          abs(balance_step(0,u,s,.5)-u)<1e-12,
          abs(balance_step(1,u,s,.5)-1)<1e-12)


The all-a boundary remains fixed because this one-way mutation model cannot recreate A. Our interior equilibrium comparison starts away from that boundary. Changing the order of mutation and selection changes the exact recursion, so the life cycle must accompany the formula.

title: Mutation, selection and drift at balance
section: 2. Find equilibria and compare familiar expressions
text:
2. Find equilibria and compare familiar expressions
An interior equilibrium satisfies \(q'=q\). For a rare deleterious allele with \(h>0\), the usual small-rate expression is \(q\approx u/(hs)\). For complete recessivity it is \(q\approx\sqrt{u/s}\); see the theoretical discussion of selection versus transmission.
For our specific one-way mutation-after-selection recursion with \(h=0\), the equilibrium equation factors as \((1-q)(u-sq^2)=0\). Thus its interior root is exactly \(\sqrt{u/s}\) when \(u<s\). That exact equality is a property of this declared life cycle, not permission to treat the square-root expression as exact under every model.


Show R code
h_values <- c(Recessive=0,Intermediate=.5)
equilibrium <- vapply(h_values,function(h)
  uniroot(function(q) balance_step(q,u,s,h)-q,c(0,.5),tol=1e-12)$root,
  numeric(1))
approximation <- c(Recessive=sqrt(u/s),Intermediate=u/(.5*s))
stopifnot(abs(equilibrium["Recessive"]-sqrt(u/s))<1e-10,
          max(abs(vapply(seq_along(h_values),function(i)
            balance_step(equilibrium[i],u,s,h_values[i])-equilibrium[i],
            numeric(1))))<1e-10)
knitr::kable(data.frame(model=names(h_values),h=unname(h_values),
  exact_equilibrium=unname(equilibrium),rare_allele_expression=unname(approximation)),

title: Mutation, selection and drift at balance
section: 3. Declare a neutral two-allele mutation–drift model
text:
3. Declare a neutral two-allele mutation–drift model
Now use a different model: no selection, two alleles A/a, and symmetric reversible mutation at rate \(\mu\) in each direction. A diploid Wright–Fisher population has \(N\) individuals and \(M=2N\) sampled copies. Conditional on current a frequency \(q\), the pool frequency after mutation is
\[q_m=\mu+(1-2\mu)q.\]
The next copy count is \(K'\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(M,q_m)\). At positive mutation, counts zero and \(M\) can be left again. The number \(N\) here defines the idealized sampling model; it is not an effective population-size estimate from a census or a real breeding programme.


Show R code
N <- 5L; M <- 2*N; mu <- .05
states <- 0:M
grid <- states/M
pool <- mu+(1-2*mu)*grid
P <- t(vapply(pool,function(q) dbinom(states,size=M,prob=q),numeric(M+1L)))
dimnames(P) <- list(current=states,next_count=states)
stopifnot(max(abs(rowSums(P)-1))<1e-12,
          max(abs(drop(P %*% grid)-pool))<1e-12,
          P[1,2]>0,P[M+1,M]>0)


The small population and relatively large mutation rate keep the finite distribution visible. They are chosen for teaching, not realistic values for a nucleotide mutation process.

title: Mutation, selection and drift at balance
text:
4. Calculate the stationary distribution
A stationary probability vector \(\pi\) satisfies \(\pi^TP=\pi^T\) and sums to one. It describes the distribution over count states after equilibration, not a constant allele count in each generation. Solve the finite system exactly up to numerical precision.


Show R code
system <- t(P)-diag(M+1L)
system[M+1L,] <- 1
rhs <- c(rep(0,M),1)
stationary <- drop(solve(system,rhs))
stopifnot(all(stationary>0),abs(sum(stationary)-1)<1e-12,
          max(abs(drop(stationary %*% P)-stationary))<1e-12,
          abs(sum(stationary*grid)-.5)<1e-12)

title: Mutation, selection and drift at balance
section: 5. Derive the diversity balance for this model
text:
5. Derive the diversity balance for this model
Let \(H(q)=2q(1-q)\), the probability that two independently drawn gene copies with replacement differ at this biallelic locus. It is the same marker-frequency definition used in earlier practicals, not a realized diploid genotype count.
Mutation gives
\[H(q_m)=2\mu(1-\mu)+(1-2\mu)^2H(q).\]
Binomial sampling multiplies its conditional expectation by \(c=1-1/M\). Therefore
\[E(H_{t+1})=c\left[2\mu(1-\mu)+(1-2\mu)^2E(H_t)\right].\]
The stationary value is
\[\overline H=
\frac{c\,2\mu(1-\mu)}{1-c(1-2\mu)^2}.\]


Show R code
c_drift <- 1-1/M
H <- 2*grid*(1-grid)
H_stationary <- c_drift*2*mu*(1-mu)/(1-c_drift*(1-2*mu)^2)
H_from_distribution <- sum(stationary*H)
H_from_mean_frequency <- 2*.5*(1-.5)
stopifnot(abs(H_stationary-H_from_distribution)<1e-12,
  max(abs(drop(P %*% H)-c_drift*(2*mu*(1-mu)+(1-2*mu)^2*H)))<1e-12,
  H_from_distribution<H_from_mean_frequency)
c(stationary_mean_HE=H_from_distribution,HE_at_mean_frequency=H_from_mean_frequency)

The matrix calculation independently verifies the moment recursion in every count state. A small number of simulated paths would not be needed to estimate this stationary expectation, because the complete finite distribution is available here.
Question 1. Why does stationary mean frequency 0.5 not imply mean heterozygosity 0.5?






Suggested answer





Frequency varies across stationary populations. Since \(E[2q(1-q)]=2E(q)(1-E(q))-2\operatorname{Var}(q)\), the mean diversity is below the value calculated at the mean frequency whenever frequencies vary. Averaging a nonlinear summary requires averaging the summary itself.

section: 6. Match the diversity formula to the mutation model
text:
6. Match the diversity formula to the mutation model
The slide expression \(4N_e\mu/(1+4N_e\mu)\) is a familiar neutral mutation–drift approximation when mutation creates new allele identities under an infinite-alleles model. See the infinite-alleles comparison in Engelstädter (2017). It is not the exact formula for the reversible two-allele process above. A two-allele independent-copy diversity measure cannot exceed 0.5, whereas an infinite-alleles measure can exceed 0.5 because there can be more than two states.

title: Mutation, selection and drift at balance
section: 7. Equilibrium and stationarity answer different questions
text:
7. Equilibrium and stationarity answer different questions
The mutation–selection example has an interior deterministic frequency at which opposing changes balance. The finite neutral example has a stationary distribution in which individual populations keep changing. Adding both selection and drift to the same model creates another problem: its stationary or transient behavior must be evaluated under that combined transition model.
Without mutation, the neutral finite process has absorbing loss and fixation states. With positive reversible mutation, those states are not absorbing. An allele can be absent in one sampled generation and reintroduced later; positive long-run diversity does not require polymorphism in every population at every time.

In the deterministic model, remove selection and derive the one-way mutation trajectory. What happens to the interior mutation–selection balance?

mean_q <- sum(stationary*grid)
variance_q <- sum(stationary*(grid-mean_q)^2)
stopifnot(abs(H_from_distribution-(2*mean_q*(1-mean_q)-2*variance_q))<1e-12)

title: Conservation genetics and management choices
section: 1. Specify the candidate parents and ancestral base
text:
1. Specify the candidate parents and ancestral base
There are two male and two female candidates. M1 and F1 are full siblings from one pair of unrelated, noninbred founders. M2 and F2 are full siblings from another founder pair. All four founders are mutually unrelated. Each candidate therefore has inbreeding coefficient zero, while full siblings have kinship \(1/4\).
Kinship \(\phi_{ij}\) is the probability that an allele drawn from individual \(i\) and one drawn from \(j\) are identical by descent on this ancestral base. Its diagonal is \((1+F_i)/2\). The additive relationship matrix is \(A=2\phi\). Expected inbreeding in a child is the kinship between its parents:
\[F_{\mathrm{child}}=\phi_{\mathrm{sire,dam}}.\]
QG Practical 9 derives relationships from pedigrees. Here the small matrix is supplied directly, so no sibling repository or extra R package is required.


Show R code
ids <- c("M1", "M2", "F1", "F2")
phi <- diag(0.5, 4)
dimnames(phi) <- list(ids, ids)
phi["M1", "F1"] <- phi["F1", "M1"] <- 0.25
phi["M2", "F2"] <- phi["F2", "M2"] <- 0.25
stopifnot(isSymmetric(phi), min(eigen(phi, symmetric=TRUE)$values) > 0)

title: Conservation genetics and management choices
section: 2. Keep contributions fixed and change pairings
text:
2. Keep contributions fixed and change pairings
Each plan produces eight offspring. Within-family mating pairs full siblings; between-family mating pairs unrelated candidates. A mixed plan uses both types.


Show R code
plans <- list(
  Within = data.frame(sire=rep(c("M1","M2"), each=4),
                      dam=rep(c("F1","F2"), each=4)),
  Between = data.frame(sire=rep(c("M1","M2"), each=4),
                       dam=rep(c("F2","F1"), each=4)),
  Mixed = data.frame(sire=rep(c("M1","M1","M2","M2"), each=2),
                     dam=rep(c("F1","F2","F1","F2"), each=2))
)
contributions <- function(plan) {
  as.numeric(table(factor(c(plan$sire,plan$dam), levels=ids))) /
    (2*nrow(plan))
}
C <- t(vapply(plans, contributions, numeric(4)))
colnames(C) <- ids
stopifnot(all(abs(C-0.25)<1e-12), all(abs(rowSums(C)-1)<1e-12))

Between 0.25 0.25 0.25 0.25
Mixed   0.25 0.25 0.25 0.25


Each parent supplies four of the sixteen parental slots, giving expected genetic contribution \(c_i=1/4\). This is an expectation over Mendelian transmission; realized contributions at individual loci can differ.


Show R code
mean_F <- vapply(plans, function(plan) {
  mean(phi[cbind(match(plan$sire,ids), match(plan$dam,ids))])
}, numeric(1))
stopifnot(max(abs(mean_F-c(0.25,0,0.125)))<1e-12)

        col=c("#d95f02","#1b9e77","#7570b3"))









Interpretation question. Why does equal use of the same four parents not determine offspring inbreeding?






Suggested answer





Contributions count how often each parent is used. Inbreeding depends on which parents are paired. The within-family, between-family and mixed plans have mean expected offspring inbreeding 0.25, 0 and 0.125 respectively.

title: Conservation genetics and management choices
section: 3. Separate allele diversity from heterozygous genotypes
text:
3. Separate allele diversity from heterozygous genotypes
Supply four hypothetical biallelic markers. Dosage counts the B allele, with AA=0, AB=1 and BB=2. These are complete, known parental genotypes, rather than an HWE sample.


Show R code
D <- cbind(marker1=c(2,0,2,0), marker2=c(1,1,1,1),
           marker3=c(2,1,0,1), marker4=c(0,2,0,2))
rownames(D) <- ids
D


   marker1 marker2 marker3 marker4
M1       2       1       2       0
M2       0       1       1       2
F1       2       1       0       0
F2       0       1       1       2


For a specified parental contribution vector, expected offspring B frequency is \(p_B=\sum_i c_i d_i/2\). The frequency-based diversity measure \(H_E=2p_B(1-p_B)\) describes random union at that frequency.
For a particular mating, let \(p_s=d_s/2\) and \(p_d=d_d/2\). Mendelian transmission gives the heterozygous-child probability
\[P(AB\mid d_s,d_d)=p_s(1-p_d)+(1-p_s)p_d.\]
This is conditional on the known parents and mating arrangement. It need not equal the random-union expectation.


Show R code
expected_p <- C %*% (D/2)
expected_HE <- 2*expected_p*(1-expected_p)
expected_HO <- t(vapply(plans, function(plan) {
  ps <- D[plan$sire,,drop=FALSE]/2
  pd <- D[plan$dam,,drop=FALSE]/2
  colMeans(ps*(1-pd)+(1-ps)*pd)
}, numeric(ncol(D))))
colnames(expected_HO) <- colnames(D)
stopifnot(all(abs(expected_p-0.5)<1e-12),
          max(abs(rowMeans(expected_HO)-c(0.3125,0.75,0.53125)))<1e-12)
data.frame(plan=names(plans), mean_HE=rowMeans(expected_HE),
           expected_heterozygous_fraction=rowMeans(expected_HO),
           mean_offspring_F=mean_F, row.names=NULL)


     plan mean_HE expected_heterozygous_fraction mean_offspring_F
1  Within     0.5                        0.31250            0.250
2 Between     0.5                        0.75000            0.000
3   Mixed     0.5                        0.53125            0.125


The between-family plan has expected heterozygous fraction 0.75 across this panel, although \(H_E=0.5\) for every marker. Pairing opposite homozygotes can make all offspring heterozygous at a marker. This does not violate the maximum of 0.5 for the random-union two-allele expression.
Do not convert this small panel’s heterozygous fraction into pedigree inbreeding. Marker states describe identity by state; pedigree kinship describes identity by descent. Neither calculation here estimates genome-wide diversity from real samples.

title: Conservation genetics and management choices
text:
4. Measure concentration and group coancestry
The effective number of contributors \(1/\sum_i c_i^2\) is a concentration descriptor. It equals four when four parents contribute equally. It is not an estimate of effective population size \(N_e\).
Group coancestry is
\[\Theta=\sum_i\sum_j c_i c_j\phi_{ij}=c^\mathsf{T}\phi c.\]
It is the expected kinship of two parental identities sampled independently with probabilities \(c_i\). Sampling is with replacement, so the diagonal contributes. This quantity uses contributions and the kinship matrix, while immediate offspring inbreeding also uses the mating arrangement.


Show R code
contributors <- 1/rowSums(C^2)
group_coancestry <- rowSums((C %*% phi)*C)
stopifnot(all(abs(contributors-4)<1e-12),
          all(abs(group_coancestry-0.1875)<1e-12))
data.frame(plan=names(plans), contributors, group_coancestry,
           mean_offspring_F=mean_F, row.names=NULL)


     plan contributors group_coancestry mean_offspring_F
1  Within            4           0.1875            0.250
2 Between            4           0.1875            0.000
3   Mixed            4           0.1875            0.125


All three plans have the same group coancestry. Avoiding related pairings reduces immediate offspring inbreeding without changing this parental contribution measure. It does not establish that future generations will retain the same diversity.
Exercise. Use only M1 and F1, each with contribution 0.5. Calculate the concentration descriptor and group coancestry. Which founder family disappears from the plan?






Solution







Show R code
c_small <- c(0.5,0,0.5,0)
c(contributors=1/sum(c_small^2),
  group_coancestry=drop(t(c_small) %*% phi %*% c_small))


    contributors group_coancestry 
           2.000            0.375 


The effective number of contributors is two and group coancestry is 0.375. Founder family B is no longer represented. This describes the chosen contributions, not a population-size estimate or a forecast of extinction.

title: Conservation genetics and management choices
text:
5. Make the resource constraint explicit
Suppose offspring upkeep costs two units per child. Each between-family offspring also costs one unit for coordination. These invented costs illustrate a decision rule: among these three equal-contribution plans, minimize mean expected offspring inbreeding within the budget.


Show R code
family <- setNames(c("A","B","A","B"), ids)
cost <- vapply(plans, function(plan) {
  2*nrow(plan)+sum(family[plan$sire]!=family[plan$dam])
}, numeric(1))
comparison <- data.frame(plan=names(plans), cost,
                         mean_offspring_F=mean_F,
                         group_coancestry, row.names=NULL)
choose_plan <- function(budget) {
  feasible <- comparison[comparison$cost<=budget,,drop=FALSE]
  if (!nrow(feasible)) return(feasible)
  feasible[which.min(feasible$mean_offspring_F),,drop=FALSE]
}
stopifnot(choose_plan(20)$plan=="Mixed", choose_plan(24)$plan=="Between",
          nrow(choose_plan(15))==0)
comparison


     plan cost mean_offspring_F group_coancestry
1  Within   16            0.250           0.1875
2 Between   24            0.000           0.1875
3   Mixed   20            0.125           0.1875


Show R code
choose_plan(20)


   plan cost mean_offspring_F group_coancestry
3 Mixed   20            0.125           0.1875


At budget 20, the mixed plan is the best of the three feasible alternatives for the declared objective. At budget 24, the between-family plan is feasible and has zero expected offspring inbreeding on the specified base. Minimizing group coancestry alone would give a tie among all three plans.
This comparison enumerates supplied alternatives; it does not find a global optimum over every possible contribution and mating schedule. A real planning problem needs its own candidate information, welfare and reproductive constraints, costs and objective.

title: Conservation genetics and management choices
section: 6. Connect the one-generation decision to drift
text:
6. Connect the one-generation decision to drift
Under an idealized neutral diploid population with constant supplied \(N_e\), no mutation or migration, expected allele diversity decays as
\[H_t/H_0=\left(1-\frac{1}{2N_e}\right)^t.\]
This is the model from Practical 6. The following scenarios do not infer \(N_e\) from our four parents or their concentration descriptor.


Show R code
Ne <- c(10,50,100)
time <- 0:20
retention <- sapply(Ne, function(n) (1-1/(2*n))^time)
matplot(time, retention, type="l", lty=1, lwd=2,
        col=c("#d95f02","#1b9e77","#7570b3"),
        xlab="Generation", ylab="Expected diversity relative to generation 0")
legend("bottomleft", legend=paste("Supplied Ne =",Ne), lty=1, lwd=2,
       col=c("#d95f02","#1b9e77","#7570b3"), bty="n")









A low immediate offspring inbreeding value and sustained diversity are different targets. This practical contains no deleterious-allele fitness model, so its results cannot compare purging, genetic load or demographic recovery. Practical 9 explains how mutation and selection assumptions affect equilibrium arguments.

text:
Exercises and discussion

Change the budget to 16 and explain the selected plan.
Report each plan’s expected heterozygous fraction for marker 1. Explain the result from the four parental genotypes.
Give an example in which reducing offspring inbreeding leaves group coancestry unchanged.
State what information is missing before comparing long-term population viability.







Suggested solutions







Show R code
choose_plan(16)


    plan cost mean_offspring_F group_coancestry
1 Within   16             0.25           0.1875


Show R code
expected_HO[,"marker1"]


 Within Between   Mixed 
    0.0     1.0     0.5 


Only the within-family plan is feasible at budget 16. Marker 1 heterozygous probabilities are 0, 1 and 0.5 for within-family, between-family and mixed plans. Changing within-family to between-family pairings preserves the contribution vector and group coancestry. Long-term viability requires reproductive and demographic dynamics, environmental conditions and a model connecting genotypes to fitness, as well as uncertainty in the inputs.
