title: DNA profiles and match probabilities
text:
Calculate multi-allelic genotype probabilities; combine loci under an independence assumption; distinguish a fixed-profile match probability from agreement between two random profiles; examine population structure; and interpret a likelihood ratio under explicit source hypotheses.
This practical follows the slides on DNA forensics. Review allele frequencies and HWE, population structure and linkage disequilibrium.
Every frequency and profile below is hypothetical. We assume autosomal diploid loci, a complete single-source profile, correct allele calls, random union within the declared population and an unrelated alternative contributor. These calculations illustrate population-genetics reasoning rather than an operational forensic analysis.

title: DNA profiles and match probabilities
text:
Calculate multi-allelic genotype probabilities; combine loci under an independence assumption; distinguish a fixed-profile match probability from agreement between two random profiles; examine population structure; and interpret a likelihood ratio under explicit source hypotheses.
This practical follows the slides on DNA forensics. Review allele frequencies and HWE, population structure and linkage disequilibrium.
Every frequency and profile below is hypothetical. We assume autosomal diploid loci, a complete single-source profile, correct allele calls, random union within the declared population and an unrelated alternative contributor. These calculations illustrate population-genetics reasoning rather than an operational forensic analysis.

title: DNA profiles and match probabilities
text:
1. Describe a multi-allelic profile
An STR allele label identifies a marker state; it is not a count of B alleles. A diploid genotype contains two labels at each locus. Our three teaching loci each have three possible alleles. The same label at different loci has no implication of shared ancestry.


Show R code
frequencies <- list(
  L1=c(`10`=0.5, `11`=0.3, `12`=0.2),
  L2=c(`8`=0.6, `9`=0.3, `10`=0.1),
  L3=c(`14`=0.4, `15`=0.4, `16`=0.2)
)
profile <- list(L1=c("10","12"), L2=c("9","9"), L3=c("14","16"))
stopifnot(identical(names(profile),names(frequencies)))
data.frame(locus=names(profile),
           genotype=vapply(profile,paste,character(1),collapse=" / "))


   locus genotype
L1    L1  10 / 12
L2    L2    9 / 9
L3    L3  14 / 16


Treat the supplied frequencies as known parameters for this exercise. Reference databases in applications estimate them; finite sample size, sampling design and rare alleles introduce further uncertainty.

title: DNA profiles and match probabilities
text:
2. Calculate genotype probabilities
Under random union, a homozygote \(a/a\) has probability \(p_a^2\). A heterozygote \(a/b\) has probability \(2p_ap_b\): either parental ordering produces the same unordered genotype.


Show R code
check_frequencies <- function(p) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(p),length(p)>0,!is.null(names(p)),
            !anyDuplicated(names(p)),all(is.finite(p)),all(p>=0),
            abs(sum(p)-1)<1e-12)
}
genotype_probability <- function(g,p) {
  check_frequencies(p)
  stopifnot(length(g)==2,all(g %in% names(p)))
  if (g[1]==g[2]) unname(p[g[1]]^2) else unname(2*p[g[1]]*p[g[2]])
}
probabilities <- vapply(names(profile), function(locus) {
  genotype_probability(profile[[locus]],frequencies[[locus]])
}, numeric(1))
stopifnot(max(abs(probabilities-c(0.2,0.09,0.16)))<1e-12,
          genotype_probability(c("12","10"),frequencies$L1)==probabilities[1])
probabilities


  L1   L2   L3 
0.20 0.09 0.16 


Verify that all possible unordered genotypes at each locus exhaust probability one.


Show R code
all_genotypes <- function(p) {
  pairs <- expand.grid(a=names(p),b=names(p),stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
  pairs <- pairs[match(pairs$a,names(p))<=match(pairs$b,names(p)),]
  pairs$probability <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(pairs)),function(i) {
    genotype_probability(c(pairs$a[i],pairs$b[i]),p)
  },numeric(1))
  pairs
}
stopifnot(all(vapply(frequencies,function(p) {
  abs(sum(all_genotypes(p)$probability)-1)<1e-12
},logical(1))))
all_genotypes(frequencies$L1)


   a  b probability
1 10 10        0.25
4 10 11        0.30
5 11 11        0.09
7 10 12        0.20
8 11 12        0.12
9 12 12        0.04


Question. Why is the heterozygote probability doubled, while the homozygote probability is not?






Suggested answer





For distinct alleles there are two ordered draws, a then b and b then a. For identical alleles there is only the a then a event. Counting it twice would make the genotype distribution sum to more than one.

title: DNA profiles and match probabilities
section: 3. Combine independent loci for a fixed profile
text:
3. Combine independent loci for a fixed profile
If genotypes at the loci are independent in the declared population, the probability that one unrelated random individual has this specified profile is
\[r=P(G=g)=\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}P(G_\ell=g_\ell).\]


Show R code
rmp <- prod(probabilities)
stopifnot(abs(rmp-0.00288)<1e-12)
c(random_match_probability=rmp, reciprocal=1/rmp)


random_match_probability               reciprocal 
                 0.00288                347.22222 


Show R code
barplot(-log10(probabilities),names.arg=names(probabilities),
        ylab="Contribution to -log10(profile probability)",col="#1b9e77")









The toy profile probability is 0.00288, about one in 347 under these assumptions. This deliberately short teaching panel does not illustrate the discriminatory power of a real marker panel. Multiplying probabilities requires independence; counting an identical duplicate marker twice would square a probability without adding information.
For many loci, summing log probabilities avoids numerical underflow: \(\log r=\sum_\ell\log P(G_\ell=g_\ell)\).


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(exp(sum(log(probabilities)))-rmp)<1e-12)



Two random profiles answer a different question
If two people are drawn independently from the same genotype distribution, their probability of matching at a locus is \(\sum_g P(g)^2\). Across independent loci, multiply these sums.


Show R code
pair_match <- prod(vapply(frequencies,function(p) {
  sum(all_genotypes(p)$probability^2)
},numeric(1)))
c(fixed_profile=rmp,two_random_profiles=pair_match)


      fixed_profile two_random_profiles 
         0.00288000          0.01275916 


The first calculation conditions on the supplied profile. The second averages over every possible first profile, including common ones. They need not coincide.

title: DNA profiles and match probabilities
section: 4. Population structure changes the product calculation
text:
4. Population structure changes the product calculation
Imagine two hypothetical subpopulations, equally represented in a sampling population. Individuals belong to one subpopulation at all three loci. Genotypes are independent across loci within each subpopulation.


Show R code
pop_A <- frequencies
pop_B <- list(L1=c(`10`=0.2,`11`=0.3,`12`=0.5),
              L2=c(`8`=0.2,`9`=0.5,`10`=0.3),
              L3=c(`14`=0.7,`15`=0.2,`16`=0.1))
profile_probability <- function(freq) {
  prod(vapply(names(profile),function(locus) {
    genotype_probability(profile[[locus]],freq[[locus]])
  },numeric(1)))
}
pooled <- Map(function(a,b) (a+b)/2,pop_A,pop_B)
correct_mixture <- 0.5*profile_probability(pop_A)+0.5*profile_probability(pop_B)
pooled_HWE_product <- profile_probability(pooled)
# Even multiplying the correct marginal genotype probabilities loses shared ancestry.
marginal_product <- prod(vapply(names(profile),function(locus) {
  0.5*genotype_probability(profile[[locus]],pop_A[[locus]])+
    0.5*genotype_probability(profile[[locus]],pop_B[[locus]])
},numeric(1)))
stopifnot(abs(correct_mixture-0.00494)<1e-12,
          abs(pooled_HWE_product-correct_mixture)>1e-6,
          abs(marginal_product-correct_mixture)>1e-6)
c(mixture_of_profile_probabilities=correct_mixture,
  pooled_frequency_HWE_product=pooled_HWE_product,
  product_of_marginal_genotype_probabilities=marginal_product)


          mixture_of_profile_probabilities 
                                  0.004940 
              pooled_frequency_HWE_product 
                                  0.006468 
product_of_marginal_genotype_probabilities 
                                  0.005100 


The mixture calculation first computes the complete profile probability within each population, then averages. Pooled allele frequencies assume random union across the mixture. Even using correct marginal genotype probabilities and multiplying them omits the common population membership across loci. Unlinked loci can therefore be statistically dependent in a pooled population.
This example exposes an assumption rather than prescribing a correction for casework. It also does not supply the conditional distribution for a relative of the reference individual.

title: DNA profiles and match probabilities
text:
5. Specify hypotheses before interpreting evidence
Condition on the reference individual’s known profile \(g\). Define two source hypotheses:

\(H_S\): the reference individual supplied the single-source sample.
\(H_U\): an unrelated random individual from the declared population supplied it.

Let \(E\) be observing a complete matching profile. In the idealized error-free model, \(P(E\mid H_S,g)=1\) and \(P(E\mid H_U,g)=r\). Consequently,
\[LR=\frac{P(E\mid H_S,g)}{P(E\mid H_U,g)}=\frac{1}{r}.\]


Show R code
LR <- 1/rmp
LR


[1] 347.2222


The reciprocal relationship holds for these particular hypotheses and observation assumptions. A related alternative contributor, uncertain calls or a mixture requires a different probability model. NIST’s DNA-mixture explainer describes why mixtures and low-level samples involve additional interpretation.
A likelihood ratio compares probabilities of evidence under hypotheses. It is not a probability that a source hypothesis is true. To illustrate the algebra, supply hypothetical prior source probabilities and apply Bayes’ rule:
\[P(H_S\mid E,g)=\frac{LR\,\pi}{LR\,\pi+(1-\pi)},\]
where \(\pi=P(H_S\mid g)\) and the two hypotheses exhaust this teaching model.


Show R code
prior <- c(0.001,0.01,0.5)
posterior <- LR*prior/(LR*prior+1-prior)
data.frame(hypothetical_prior=prior,posterior_source_probability=posterior)


  hypothetical_prior posterior_source_probability
1              0.001                    0.2579234
2              0.010                    0.7781375
3              0.500                    0.9971283


The same LR gives different posteriors for different priors. These invented priors are not assigned to an actual person. Source attribution also does not specify how, when or why DNA arrived, or establish guilt. For the statistical distinctions, see the National Research Council’s Statistical Issues chapter.

title: DNA profiles and match probabilities
text:
6. Searching many unrelated profiles
For a fixed target profile and \(N\) independent unrelated draws with match probability \(r\), the expected number of matches is \(Nr\). The probability of at least one is
\[1-(1-r)^N.\]


Show R code
N <- c(1,100,1000)
data.frame(draws=N,expected_matches=N*rmp,
           probability_at_least_one=-expm1(N*log1p(-rmp)))


  draws expected_matches probability_at_least_one
1     1          0.00288                0.0028800
2   100          0.28800                0.2505499
3  1000          2.88000                0.9440980


This sampling exercise assumes independent draws from the specified population. It is not a database-search likelihood ratio or a posterior about someone selected by a search; those questions must include the selection procedure and hypotheses.

title: DNA profiles and match probabilities
text:
Exercises

Replace L2’s genotype with 8/9 and recompute the fixed-profile probability.
Explain why multiplying probabilities for a marker and its identical duplicate is incorrect.
Explain why the pooled-frequency calculation and the mixture calculation differ.
Under which assumptions is the LR exactly the reciprocal of the match probability?







Suggested solutions







Show R code
changed <- profile
changed$L2 <- c("8","9")
changed_rmp <- prod(vapply(names(changed),function(locus) {
  genotype_probability(changed[[locus]],frequencies[[locus]])
},numeric(1)))
stopifnot(abs(changed_rmp-0.01152)<1e-12)
changed_rmp


[1] 0.01152


The new probability is 0.01152. A duplicate marker is perfectly dependent on the first. Mixture membership is shared across loci, and pooling alleles also changes the random-union model. The reciprocal LR requires a matching, complete, correctly called single-source profile, a known reference profile, certainty of a match under the same-source hypothesis and the stated unrelated-random-source alternative.

title: Sequence divergence and the molecular clock
text:
Count differences on a declared alignment denominator; distinguish observed differences from substitution distance; apply a simple correction for repeated substitutions; convert a per-lineage rate to pairwise time; and examine sampling and calibration uncertainty.
This practical follows the molecular-clock slides. Review genotype data, genetic diversity and mutation. All sequences, rates and calibrations below are hypothetical. The examples use base R without downloads.

title: Sequence divergence and the molecular clock
text:
Count differences on a declared alignment denominator; distinguish observed differences from substitution distance; apply a simple correction for repeated substitutions; convert a per-lineage rate to pairwise time; and examine sampling and calibration uncertainty.
This practical follows the molecular-clock slides. Review genotype data, genetic diversity and mutation. All sequences, rates and calibrations below are hypothetical. The examples use base R without downloads.

title: Sequence divergence and the molecular clock
text:
1. Declare the comparable sites
An alignment specifies which positions are homologous. Here it is supplied rather than inferred. Count a difference only where both sequences have an unambiguous A, C, G or T. N and gaps are excluded; report their number rather than treating them as matches.


Show R code
sequence_A <- strsplit("ACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGT", "")[[1]]
sequence_B <- sequence_A
sequence_B[c(3,11,25,33)] <- c("A","A","T","G")
sequence_B[c(5,6)] <- c("N","-")
comparable <- sequence_A %in% c("A","C","G","T") &
              sequence_B %in% c("A","C","G","T")
L <- sum(comparable)
K <- sum(sequence_A[comparable]!=sequence_B[comparable])
p_hat <- K/L
stopifnot(L==38,K==4)
data.frame(aligned_positions=length(sequence_A),excluded=sum(!comparable),
           comparable=L,differences=K,observed_fraction=p_hat)


  aligned_positions excluded comparable differences observed_fraction
1                40        2         38           4         0.1052632


The observed fraction \(\hat p=K/L\) is often called the p-distance. It records different present-day states. It does not count every substitution along the path: a site can change more than once or return to its initial state.
Our exclusion rule defines the analysis set. If missing sites differ systematically from retained sites, this set need not represent the whole sequence. Multiple pairwise comparisons also require attention to whether their denominators cover the same positions.

title: Sequence divergence and the molecular clock
section: 2. Correct under a specified substitution model
text:
2. Correct under a specified substitution model
The Jukes–Cantor model assumes equal equilibrium base frequencies, equal instantaneous rates between distinct bases and a constant rate across sites and along the compared path. If \(d\) is expected substitutions per site along that path,
\[p(d)=\frac34\left(1-e^{-4d/3}\right).\]
Inverting gives the distance estimate
\[\hat d=-\frac34\log\left(1-\frac43\hat p\right),\qquad 0\leq\hat p<\frac34.\]
This is a model-based correction, not a reconstruction of individual historical changes. The formula and finite-sample distance-estimation issues are discussed in Improved variance estimators for one- and two-parameter models of nucleotide substitution.


Show R code
jc_distance <- function(p) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(p),all(is.finite(p)),all(p>=0),all(p<0.75))
  -0.75*log1p(-4*p/3)
}
jc_difference <- function(d) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(d),all(is.finite(d)),all(d>=0))
  -0.75*expm1(-4*d/3)
}
d_hat <- jc_distance(p_hat)
stopifnot(d_hat>p_hat,abs(jc_difference(d_hat)-p_hat)<1e-12,
          jc_distance(0)==0)
c(observed_difference=p_hat,corrected_distance=d_hat)


observed_difference  corrected_distance 
          0.1052632           0.1134232 




Show R code
d_grid <- seq(0,3,length.out=200)
plot(d_grid,jc_difference(d_grid),type="l",lwd=2,col="#1b9e77",
     xlab="Path distance: expected substitutions per site",
     ylab="Expected fraction of different bases",ylim=c(0,0.8))
abline(h=0.75,lty=2)
points(d_hat,p_hat,pch=19)









At large distances, differences approach 0.75 even while substitutions continue accumulating. Near that limit, small changes in observed differences imply large changes in corrected distance. At or above 0.75, this inverse has no finite nonnegative distance estimate. Our helper rejects that input; it does not silently truncate it.
Question. Does the correction establish that these short sequences evolved under Jukes–Cantor?






Suggested answer





No. The correction assumes the model. The short example illustrates its algebra and is not a model adequacy assessment. Unequal base composition, unequal substitution types or variation among sites may require other models.

title: Sequence divergence and the molecular clock
section: 3. Keep rate units and the two-lineage factor explicit
text:
3. Keep rate units and the two-lineage factor explicit
Let \(r\) be the substitution rate per site per lineage per generation. Two lineages accumulating changes at this same rate for \(t\) generations have total path distance
\[d=rt+rt=2rt,\qquad t=d/(2r).\]
A substitution rate describes evolutionary changes along a lineage. Equating it to a mutation rate requires an appropriate neutral model and assumptions; we supply a hypothetical substitution rate directly here.


Show R code
rate <- 1e-8
# Generation length is supplied in years per generation.
generation_years <- 2
time_generations <- d_hat/(2*rate)
time_years <- time_generations*generation_years
data.frame(distance=d_hat,rate_per_site_per_lineage_per_generation=rate,
           generations=time_generations,years=time_years)


   distance rate_per_site_per_lineage_per_generation generations    years
1 0.1134232                                    1e-08     5671161 11342323


Show R code
stopifnot(abs(2*rate*time_generations-d_hat)<1e-12)


The rate is per site, matching the distance units. The alignment length does not enter the conversion again. If a supplied rate were already a pairwise rate, another factor of two would be incorrect. For unequal lineage rates, \(d=(r_1+r_2)t\) under the corresponding constant-rate model.
This path-time calculation dates the common ancestry of the compared sequences under the model. A species split is a different event: ancestral polymorphism can make sequence common ancestry older than population separation. The simple example has no ancestral-population model, so its result is not a species-divergence estimate.

title: Sequence divergence and the molecular clock
text:
4. Calibrate and examine sensitivity
Suppose an independent comparison has a known hypothetical path-time of two million generations and corrected distance 0.04. Under the same strict two-lineage clock, it calibrates \(r=0.04/(2\times2{,}000{,}000)\).


Show R code
calibration_distance <- 0.04
calibration_generations <- 2e6
calibrated_rate <- calibration_distance/(2*calibration_generations)
stopifnot(abs(calibrated_rate-rate)<1e-20)
calibration_times <- c(1.5e6,2e6,2.5e6)
calibration_rates <- calibration_distance/(2*calibration_times)
data.frame(calibration_generations=calibration_times,
           inferred_rate=calibration_rates,
           target_generations=d_hat/(2*calibration_rates))


  calibration_generations inferred_rate target_generations
1                 1500000  1.333333e-08            4253371
2                 2000000  1.000000e-08            5671161
3                 2500000  8.000000e-09            7088952


An older calibration at the same distance implies a slower rate and an older target time. These are sensitivity scenarios, not confidence limits. Transfer of a rate between comparisons assumes the same relevant evolutionary rate; this practical does not fit a relaxed clock or a phylogenetic tree.

title: Sequence divergence and the molecular clock
text:
5. Isolate finite-site sampling uncertainty
For this exercise, assume the \(L\) retained sites are independent and share a common mismatch probability. Then \(K\) is binomial. An exact binomial interval for \(p\) can be transformed to distance and time when its endpoints remain below 0.75.


Show R code
p_interval <- unname(binom.test(K,L)$conf.int)
stopifnot(p_interval[2]<0.75)
d_interval <- jc_distance(p_interval)
t_interval <- d_interval/(2*rate)
data.frame(quantity=c("Mismatch probability","Distance","Generations"),
           estimate=c(p_hat,d_hat,time_generations),
           lower=c(p_interval[1],d_interval[1],t_interval[1]),
           upper=c(p_interval[2],d_interval[2],t_interval[2]))


              quantity     estimate        lower        upper
1 Mismatch probability 1.052632e-01 2.943452e-02 2.480494e-01
2             Distance 1.134232e-01 3.002768e-02 3.011786e-01
3          Generations 5.671161e+06 1.501384e+06 1.505893e+07


The transformed interval is conditional on independent equal-rate sites, the substitution model and the fixed rate. It does not include calibration, alignment or evolutionary-model uncertainty. If an upper endpoint reaches 0.75, a finite upper distance bound cannot be obtained by this inversion; clipping it would hide the problem.
A small seeded simulation illustrates finite-site variation at a known distance. It simulates mismatch indicators under the declared model, rather than reconstructing sequence histories.


Show R code
set.seed(1201)
true_distance <- 0.2
true_p <- jc_difference(true_distance)
lengths <- c(100,1000,10000)
replicates <- 200
estimated_p <- sapply(lengths,function(n) rbinom(replicates,n,true_p)/n)
stopifnot(all(estimated_p<0.75))
estimated_d <- matrix(jc_distance(as.vector(estimated_p)),nrow=replicates)
boxplot(as.data.frame(estimated_d),names=lengths,
        xlab="Independent retained sites",ylab="Estimated JC distance",
        col="#7570b3")
abline(h=true_distance,lty=2)









More independent sites reduce sampling variation in this example. They do not repair an incorrect clock or substitution model. The 200 draws are a teaching illustration, not a broad performance qualification.

title: Sequence divergence and the molecular clock
text:
Exercises

Estimate time from raw p-distance instead of corrected distance. Explain the direction of the difference.
Double the per-lineage rate while keeping distance fixed.
Calculate the JC distance at mismatch fraction 0.7, and explain why estimates near 0.75 are unstable.
Describe why a sequence common-ancestor time need not equal a species split time.







Suggested solutions







Show R code
c(time_from_raw_fraction=p_hat/(2*rate),
  time_from_corrected_distance=d_hat/(2*rate),
  time_at_double_rate=d_hat/(4*rate),
  distance_at_p_0.7=jc_distance(0.7))


      time_from_raw_fraction time_from_corrected_distance 
                5.263158e+06                 5.671161e+06 
         time_at_double_rate            distance_at_p_0.7 
                2.835581e+06                 2.031038e+00 


The raw fraction gives a smaller time under this model because it omits repeated substitutions. Doubling rate halves time. The correction grows rapidly near saturation: its derivative is \(1/(1-4p/3)\). Lineages sampled from different species can trace back through an ancestral population before the species separation; dating that process needs additional assumptions and information.

title: Sequence divergence and the molecular clock
text:
Package connections and next steps
These base R examples expose evolutionary-distance and sampling assumptions relevant to population-genetics teaching. They do not assume a gpop molecular-dating API. gsim breeding inheritance and gsel selection-policy responsibilities do not turn them into phylogenetic dating tools.
A further extension could compare an explicit unequal-rate model or add an ancestral coalescent model. Each changes the meaning of the estimated time and should be introduced as a new model rather than another unit conversion.

title: Disease alleles, penetrance and population risk
text:
Distinguish allele frequency, heterozygote frequency and phenotype probability; apply genotype-specific penetrance; examine an inbreeding model; distinguish population averages from known-parent crosses; and identify why phenotype prevalence alone may not identify an allele frequency.

title: Disease alleles, penetrance and population risk
text:

This practical follows population genetics in medicine, building on HWE and structure and inbreeding. Every parameter is hypothetical and describes an invented single-locus phenotype. The examples use base R and are not estimates for a named disease or an individual.

title: Disease alleles, penetrance and population risk
section: 1. Define the allele and the observation window
text:
1. Define the allele and the observation window
Let a have frequency \(q\) and A frequency \(p=1-q\) at an autosomal diploid locus. Under random union, genotype probabilities are \(p^2,2pq,q^2\) for AA, Aa and aa.
For this example, call Aa a heterozygous carrier of a. An aa individual has two copies and is reported separately. Keep the counted allele and genotype labels explicit.


Show R code
q <- 0.02
genotype_frequencies <- function(q,F=0) {
  stopifnot(length(q)==1,is.finite(q),q>=0,q<=1,
            length(F)==1,is.finite(F),F>=0,F<=1)
  p <- 1-q
  c(AA=p^2+F*p*q,Aa=2*p*q*(1-F),aa=q^2+F*p*q)
}
freq <- genotype_frequencies(q)
stopifnot(abs(sum(freq)-1)<1e-12,
          max(abs(freq-c(0.9604,0.0392,0.0004)))<1e-12)
data.frame(genotype=names(freq),probability=unname(freq),
           expected_in_100000=100000*unname(freq))


  genotype probability expected_in_100000
1       AA      0.9604              96040
2       Aa      0.0392               3920
3       aa      0.0004                 40


The expected counts are averages over hypothetical samples; they do not require every sample to contain exactly these numbers.
Define \(f_g=P(Y=1\mid G=g)\) as the probability of the specified phenotype by a declared age or observation window. These genotype-specific probabilities are the penetrance inputs. They describe whether the phenotype occurs, rather than its severity. MedlinePlus explains reduced penetrance and variable expressivity.

title: Disease alleles, penetrance and population risk
text:
2. Average genotype-specific phenotype probabilities
The population phenotype probability is
\[K=P(Y=1)=\sum_g P(G=g)f_g.\]
In a fully penetrant, purely recessive model, \(f_{AA}=f_{Aa}=0\) and \(f_{aa}=1\). Only with these assumptions and HWE does \(K=q^2\).


Show R code
full_recessive <- c(AA=0,Aa=0,aa=1)
incomplete <- c(AA=0,Aa=0,aa=0.8)
background <- c(AA=0.001,Aa=0.001,aa=0.8)
phenotype_probability <- function(freq,penetrance) {
  stopifnot(identical(names(freq),names(penetrance)),
            all(is.finite(freq)),all(freq>=0),abs(sum(freq)-1)<1e-12,
            all(is.finite(penetrance)),all(penetrance>=0),all(penetrance<=1))
  sum(freq*penetrance)
}
models <- list(Full_recessive=full_recessive,Incomplete=incomplete,
               Background=background)
K <- vapply(models,function(f) phenotype_probability(freq,f),numeric(1))
stopifnot(max(abs(K-c(0.0004,0.00032,0.0013196)))<1e-12)
K


Full_recessive     Incomplete     Background 
     0.0004000      0.0003200      0.0013196 


The background model allows the same phenotype in people without aa through causes outside this locus. It does not classify those causes or assign a clinical diagnosis. Its parameters must refer to the same observation window and sampling population.
Question. Does an aa genotype guarantee the phenotype in the incomplete model?






Suggested answer





No. Its supplied phenotype probability is 0.8. Conversely, in the background model the phenotype can occur without aa. Genotype, phenotype and inferred cause are distinct.

title: Disease alleles, penetrance and population risk
text:
3. Inbreeding changes genotype frequencies
Under the inbreeding model on a specified ancestral base,
\[P(AA)=p^2+Fpq,\quad P(Aa)=2pq(1-F),\quad P(aa)=q^2+Fpq.\]
This preserves allele frequency while shifting heterozygote probability into both homozygote classes. Here \(F\) is a supplied model parameter, not inferred from phenotype prevalence or a heterozygosity deficit.


Show R code
F_values <- c(0,0.01,0.0625)
comparison <- do.call(rbind,lapply(F_values,function(F) {
  g <- genotype_frequencies(q,F)
  stopifnot(abs(g["aa"]+g["Aa"]/2-q)<1e-12)
  data.frame(F=F,heterozygote=unname(g["Aa"]),aa=unname(g["aa"]),
             phenotype=phenotype_probability(g,background))
}))
comparison


       F heterozygote       aa   phenotype
1 0.0000     0.039200 0.000400 0.001319600
2 0.0100     0.038808 0.000596 0.001476204
3 0.0625     0.036750 0.001625 0.002298375




Show R code
F_grid <- seq(0,0.1,length.out=100)
plot(F_grid,vapply(F_grid,function(F) {
  phenotype_probability(genotype_frequencies(q,F),background)
},numeric(1)),type="l",lwd=2,col="#1b9e77",
     xlab="Supplied inbreeding coefficient F",ylab="Population phenotype probability")









For this particular penetrance vector, the phenotype probability increases with F. More generally,
\[K(F)-K(0)=Fpq(f_{AA}-2f_{Aa}+f_{aa}).\]
The direction depends on genotype-specific phenotype probabilities; it is not universally positive. This one-generation model does not simulate selection, purging, demography or changes in q.


Show R code
g_F <- genotype_frequencies(q,0.0625)
change <- phenotype_probability(g_F,background)-K["Background"]
expected_change <- 0.0625*q*(1-q)*
  (background["AA"]-2*background["Aa"]+background["aa"])
stopifnot(abs(change-expected_change)<1e-12)

title: Disease alleles, penetrance and population risk
text:
4. Condition on known parents
A population-average probability does not replace a probability conditional on known parental genotypes. For Aa by Aa, each parent transmits a with probability 1/2. Mendelian transmission gives AA, Aa and aa probabilities 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4.


Show R code
cross_probabilities <- function(sire_dosage,dam_dosage) {
  stopifnot(length(sire_dosage)==1,length(dam_dosage)==1,
            sire_dosage %in% 0:2,dam_dosage %in% 0:2)
  ps <- sire_dosage/2
  pd <- dam_dosage/2
  c(AA=(1-ps)*(1-pd),Aa=ps*(1-pd)+(1-ps)*pd,aa=ps*pd)
}
carrier_cross <- cross_probabilities(1,1)
stopifnot(max(abs(carrier_cross-c(0.25,0.5,0.25)))<1e-12)
data.frame(genotype=names(carrier_cross),probability=unname(carrier_cross))


  genotype probability
1       AA        0.25
2       Aa        0.50
3       aa        0.25


Show R code
c(full_recessive=phenotype_probability(carrier_cross,full_recessive),
  incomplete=phenotype_probability(carrier_cross,incomplete),
  background=phenotype_probability(carrier_cross,background))


full_recessive     incomplete     background 
       0.25000        0.20000        0.20075 


For this cross, aa probability is 0.25 while phenotype probability in the incomplete model is 0.20. These are per-offspring probabilities under the declared model. The cross calculation needs the parental genotypes rather than the population q; no HWE assumption is needed once those genotypes are known.

title: Disease alleles, penetrance and population risk
section: 5. Reverse conditioning is a different calculation
text:
5. Reverse conditioning is a different calculation
In the background population model, Bayes’ rule gives
\[P(G=g\mid Y=1)=\frac{P(G=g)f_g}{K}.\]


Show R code
posterior_genotype <- freq*background/K["Background"]
stopifnot(abs(sum(posterior_genotype)-1)<1e-12)
data.frame(genotype=names(freq),given_phenotype=unname(posterior_genotype))


  genotype given_phenotype
1       AA      0.72779630
2       Aa      0.02970597
3       aa      0.24249773


Show R code
c(phenotype_given_aa=background["aa"],aa_given_phenotype=posterior_genotype["aa"])


phenotype_given_aa.aa aa_given_phenotype.aa 
            0.8000000             0.2424977 


Although aa has high phenotype probability, many phenotype-positive individuals in this toy population have another genotype because those genotypes are much more common. \(P(Y=1\mid aa)\) and \(P(aa\mid Y=1)\) answer different questions.
This calculation presumes that all probabilities and the population sampling scheme are appropriate. A phenotype-ascertained sample has a different genotype distribution from a random population sample; its allele frequency cannot be treated as the population frequency without accounting for sampling.

title: Disease alleles, penetrance and population risk
text:
6. Can phenotype prevalence identify q?
Only under full recessive penetrance, zero background probability and HWE does \(q=\sqrt K\). If aa penetrance is known to be f with zero background, \(q=\sqrt{K/f}\) instead. If F is nonzero, even the fully penetrant expression becomes \(K=q^2+Fq(1-q)\).


Show R code
observed_K <- 0.0004
penetrances <- c(1,0.8,0.5)
q_scenarios <- sqrt(observed_K/penetrances)
data.frame(supplied_aa_penetrance=penetrances,q=q_scenarios,
           check_K=penetrances*q_scenarios^2)


  supplied_aa_penetrance          q check_K
1                    1.0 0.02000000   4e-04
2                    0.8 0.02236068   4e-04
3                    0.5 0.02828427   4e-04


Show R code
naive_q_background <- sqrt(K["Background"])
c(true_supplied_q=q,naive_sqrt_prevalence=naive_q_background)


                 true_supplied_q naive_sqrt_prevalence.Background 
                       0.0200000                        0.0363263 


Several combinations of q and penetrance produce the same K. The naive square-root inversion in the background example overestimates the supplied q. Unknown background probability or population structure adds further ambiguity. Observing prevalence alone does not identify all these quantities.

title: Disease alleles, penetrance and population risk
text:
Exercises

Recalculate heterozygote and aa frequencies at q=0.01 under HWE.
Compute genotype and phenotype probabilities for AA by Aa using the background model.
Give a penetrance vector for which increasing F lowers phenotype probability.
State the assumptions needed to infer q as the square root of prevalence.







Suggested solutions







Show R code
genotype_frequencies(0.01)


    AA     Aa     aa 
0.9801 0.0198 0.0001 


Show R code
cross <- cross_probabilities(0,1)
cross


 AA  Aa  aa 
0.5 0.5 0.0 


Show R code
phenotype_probability(cross,background)


[1] 0.001


Show R code
heterozygote_only <- c(AA=0,Aa=1,aa=0)
c(F0=phenotype_probability(genotype_frequencies(q,0),heterozygote_only),
  F01=phenotype_probability(genotype_frequencies(q,0.1),heterozygote_only))


     F0     F01 
0.03920 0.03528 


At q=0.01, heterozygote probability is 0.0198 and aa probability is 0.0001. AA by Aa gives half AA and half Aa; its phenotype probability is 0.001 under the background model. If only heterozygotes express the phenotype, increasing F reduces its population probability. The square-root inversion requires HWE, a purely recessive fully penetrant single-locus phenotype, zero background cases and a prevalence measurement corresponding to the model’s population and observation window.

title: Disease alleles, penetrance and population risk
text:
Package connections and teaching extensions
The examples illustrate genotype-frequency expectations and conditioning relevant to gpop; they do not assume an exported medical-risk API. gsim can extend known crosses to explicit inheritance simulations, while fitness effects and selection policies require separate definitions. Penetrance is a phenotype probability and is not automatically a reproductive fitness weight.
Useful extensions include an explicitly specified age-dependent phenotype model, several alleles at one locus or a sampling model for uncertain allele frequencies. Each requires additional assumptions rather than substituting a new number into q squared.

title: Population Genetics
text:
Core Topics

Genetic data and diversity: distinguish alleles, genotypes, haplotypes and phase; calculate frequencies and diversity measures in Practicals 1–4.
Population change: compare mutation, migration, recombination, drift and selection models in Practicals 5–7.
Statistical inference and equilibrium: assess HWE proportions and distinguish deterministic balance from stationary variation in Practicals 8–9.
Applications: connect the models to conservation choices, DNA-profile probabilities, molecular clocks and genotype-specific phenotype probabilities in Practicals 10–13.

An HWE test can detect incompatibility with its sampling and null model; a departure alone cannot identify its cause. Selective-sweep signatures and worked coalescent history remain further teaching extensions rather than completed analyses in this sequence.

text:
Using the Materials
Read the slides for a conceptual overview, then use a practical to work through assumptions, equations and interpretation. Treat R as a virtual laboratory: reproduce the example, predict the effect of changing one parameter, then compare that prediction with the result. Attempt the exercises before opening the solutions.
For independent study and exam preparation, use the shared course map to choose a route and explain the population, denominator, life cycle and sampling model behind each calculation. Project analyses need their own data checks and model assessment before teaching code is adapted.
